results.pre1900_finding: Ushna (hot). The Sanskrit nighantus, as reported in a pre-1900 source, assign Withania somnifera the qualities pungent + astringent (katu/kashaya rasa) and HOT (ushna virya). No pre-1900 source I could reach gives the Sanskrit verse itself in Devanagari, so the thermal assignment is carried here on an 1891 English report of the nighantus, not on the nighantu text.
results.evidence: "It is described in the Nighantas as tonic, alterative, pungent, astringent, hot and aphrodisiac, and is recommended in rheumatism, cough, dropsy, consumption and senile debility. Chakradatta recommends it in decoction with long pepper, butter and honey in consumption and scrofula." — William Dymock, C. J. H. Warden & David Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica: A History of the Principal Drugs of Vegetable Origin Met With in British India, Vol. II, London/Bombay/Calcutta, 1891, entry WITHANIA SOMNIFERA, Dunal (Solanaceae), pp. 566-567. Full text: https://archive.org/download/b21960343_0002/b21960343_0002_djvu.txt (item https://archive.org/details/b21960343_0002). TRANSLATION-RULE DISCLOSURE: this is an English-language 1891 summary of Sanskrit nighantu material; I did NOT locate a pre-1900 Devanagari or transliterated Sanskrit text of the Bhavaprakasha / Raja Nighantu verse, and I have deliberately NOT reproduced that verse from memory. NEGATIVE CROSS-CHECK: U. C. Dutt, The Materia Medica of the Hindus, Calcutta 1877 (https://archive.org/download/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft_djvu.txt), pp. 210-211, carries Withania somnifera (Sans. Asvagandha) but assigns NO thermal quality at all — "It is regarded as tonic, alterative and aphrodisiac and is used in consumption, emaciation of children, debility from old age, rheumatism, etc." Those are action words, not a virya. The strings 'virya' and 'vipaka' occur ZERO times in Dutt's 705 KB text.
additions: RASA (pre-1900 attested): pungent (katu) and astringent (kashaya) — Dymock 1891. Database stores 'Bitter, Astringent, Sweet'. Pungent is NOT in the stored taste and bitter/sweet are NOT in the 1891 attestation. Taste column disagrees with the only pre-1900 source found.
VIPAKA: NOT FOUND in any pre-1900 source reached. Do not fill this from a modern Ayurvedic pharmacopoeia.
GUNA: NOT FOUND in any pre-1900 source reached.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS (1891, in the source's own idiom): rheumatism, cough, dropsy, consumption, senile debility, scrofula. Ainslie (Materia Indica, 1826), quoted by Dymock at ii.14: the Tamil Vytians 'suppose it to have deobstruent and diuretic qualities'.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE (1891, from Chakradatta): decoction of the root with long pepper, butter and honey. Also a ghrita — 'boiling together one part of the root with one part of clarified butter and ten of milk'. Dutt 1877 p. 211 independently records the same: decoction of asvagandha root and long pepper given with clarified butter. So the classical vehicle is FAT + MILK, not water alone, and not a capsule. Dose stated by Dymock: 'each dose contains about 30 grains of the root'.
EXTERNAL USE: leaves moistened with warm castor oil applied to carbuncle (Ainslie 1826, via Dymock 1891); Rheede's vulnerary ointment from the leaves.
CONTRAINDICATIONS: none stated in either pre-1900 source. Record as 'not stated classically', not as 'none'.

SUBSTITUTION NOTE, commercially important: Dutt 1877 (Glossary, p. 292 n.) records that in the Ashtavarga group of eight drugs, six were already unobtainable in 1877 and Asvagandha was the standing SUBSTITUTE for Meda. Ashwagandha was in use as a replacement herb, not only in its own right.

results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目 (Bencao Gangmu), 1596, Siku Quanshu recension, 卷12上 草部山草類, entry 黃耆: 「根氣味甘微温無毒」（本經）—「白水者冷補」（别錄）. Source URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷12上 (raw: https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷12上&action=raw). The entry is headed 「黃耆」{{本經上品}}. ANCIENT LAYER, independently: 神農本草經, Sun Xingyan & Sun Fengyi 孫星衍 recension, 1799, 卷一·上經: 「味甘，微溫。主癰疽久敗創，排膿止痛，大風痢疾，五痔鼠瘻，補虛，小兒百病。一名戴糝。生山谷。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw . CAUTION ON THE 1799 TRANSCRIPTION: the Wikisource heading for this entry reads 「==黃==」 — the glyph 耆 has been dropped by the transcriber. Identity is nonetheless certain from the alias 一名戴糝 and from the 名醫 note 一名戴椹、一名芰草、一名蜀脂、一名百本. Quote the BCGM line, not the heading.
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 (upper/superior grade) — stated in the BCGM head line as 「本經上品」 and confirmed by its position in 卷一·上經 of the 1799 Sun Xingyan recension. Upper grade = non-toxic, intended for prolonged daily use. This is the grade that licenses a daily-use product.

CHANNEL ENTRY 歸經: 「元素曰…入手足太隂氣分，又入手少陽足少隂命門」 — Zhang Yuansu, quoted in BCGM 1596 卷12上. Hand and Foot Taiyin (Lung + Spleen) QI DIVISION, plus Hand Shaoyang (Sanjiao) and Foot Shaoyin (Kidney)/Mingmen. The database has no column for this and the qi-fen (qi division) specificity is the whole point of the herb.
QI/FLAVOUR DYNAMICS: 「味甘氣温平，氣薄味厚，可升可降，隂中陽也」 (Zhang Yuansu, BCGM 1596). Thin qi, thick flavour, can both ascend and descend — a yang within yin.

INCOMPATIBILITIES 相惡/使: 「之才曰茯苓為之使，惡…甲、白鮮皮」 — Xu Zhicai, in BCGM 1596 卷12上. Poria (茯苓) is the guiding envoy; it is antagonised by Dictamnus root-bark (白鮮皮) and by a drug whose first glyph is a lacuna in this transcription (rendered {{SKchar|1841}}, standardly read 龜甲, tortoise plastron). DO NOT PUBLISH THE LACUNA GLYPH AS 龜 WITHOUT A CLEAN SCAN.

CONTRAINDICATION, explicitly stated: 「震亨曰…若面黒形實而瘦者服之令人胸滿」 — Zhu Zhenheng, in BCGM 1596. In the dark-complexioned, solid-bodied, thin patient it causes chest fullness. Also 「咽乾乃虚中有熱，不可服涼藥」 context and 大明's note that the white-water (白水耆) and red-water (赤水耆) grades are 涼 (cool), not warm — so PROVENANCE CHANGES THE TEMPERATURE: 「𢎞景曰出隴西者温補，出白水者冷補」 (Tao Hongjing). A Longxi-sourced root is a warming tonic; a Baishui-sourced root is a COOLING tonic. Same drug name, opposite thermal action, decided by origin.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE: 「今人但槌扁，以蜜水塗炙數次，以熟為度；亦有以鹽湯潤透，器盛於湯瓶蒸熟切用者」 (Li Shizhen, 修治, BCGM 1596). Honey-water roasting to done-ness, or salt-water steaming. Also 斆 (Lei Xiao): 「凡使勿用木耆草，真相似」 — a named adulterant warning, and Han Baosheng/Wang Haogu warn that alfalfa root (苜蓿根) is faked as huangqi and 「能令人瘦」, makes people thin, the opposite effect.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS (本經, via BCGM 1596): 癰疽久敗瘡、排膿止痛、大風癩疾、五痔鼠瘻、補虛、小兒百病 — chronic non-healing abscess and sore, expelling pus and stopping pain, severe wind/leprous disease, the five haemorrhoids, scrofulous fistula, supplementing vacuity, all childhood diseases. 別錄 adds 補丈夫虛損、五勞羸瘦、止渴腹痛洩痢、益氣利陰氣.
ROLE DOCTRINE worth surfacing in copy: 「人參補中，黃耆實表」 and 「若表虛自汗、亡陽、潰瘍、痘疹陰瘡者，當以黃耆為君，人參為臣」 (Chen Jiamo, in BCGM 1596). Astragalus is the EXTERIOR/surface drug; ginseng is the interior/centre drug.

results.pre1900_finding: The pre-1900 Chinese drug 五加皮 is 辛溫 (acrid, warm) — which WOULD confirm 'Warm' — but 五加皮 is not Eleutherococcus senticosus. Li Shizhen's 五加 is the five-leaflet shrub of the 五加 group (Acanthopanax gracilistylus and relatives), described as 「五葉交加者良」 with white flowers; E. senticosus (刺五加) is a distinct northern species that has NO separate entry in any pre-1900 materia medica I could reach. The string 刺五加 occurs ZERO times across the BCGM volumes downloaded and zero times in the 1799 Shennong recension and in Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757.
results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目, 1596, Siku Quanshu recension, 卷36 木部灌木類, entry 五加 (headed 「五加」{{本經上品}}): 「根皮（同莖）氣味辛温無毒」，「之才曰：逺志為之使，惡𤣥參、蛇皮。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷36 . SPECIES-DEFINING DESCRIPTION from the same entry, 集解: 「五加皮五葉者良」（別錄）; 「春生苖莖葉俱青作叢，赤莖又似藤葛，高三五尺，上有黒刺，葉生五枚作簇者良，四葉三葉者最多為次，三四月開白花，結青子」（蘇頌）— five leaflets, white flowers, 3-5 chi tall. That is not E. senticosus. ANCIENT LAYER: 神農本草經, Sun Xingyan recension, 1799, 卷一·上經, 五加皮: 「[味]辛，溫。主心腹疝氣，腹痛，益氣療躄，小兒不能行，疸創陰蝕。一名豺漆。」 (the transcription prints 孕 where 味 belongs — a clear transcription corruption; flagged, not silently fixed). Wu Yiluo 吳儀洛, 本草從新, 1757: 「五加皮…辛順氣而化痰，苦堅骨而益精，溫祛風而勝溼。」 https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 (upper grade) — 「本經上品」 in the BCGM head line, and the entry sits in 卷一·上經 of the 1799 recension. Applies to 五加皮, not to E. senticosus.
CHANNEL ENTRY 歸經: NOT GIVEN in BCGM 1596 for this drug. Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757 gives an organ rationale rather than a channel: 「腎得其養，則痰水去而骨壮；肝得其養，則邪風去而筋强」 — Kidney and Liver.

CONTRAINDICATION, stated explicitly (Wu Yiluo, 本草從新, 1757): 「下部無風寒溼邪而有火，及肝腎虛而有火者，勿服。」 Do not give it where there is heat in the lower body without wind-cold-damp, or where there is Liver/Kidney vacuity WITH heat. The database has no contraindication column and this one is directly product-relevant.
INCOMPATIBILITIES: 「逺志為之使，惡𤣥參、蛇皮」 (Xu Zhicai, in BCGM 1596). Polygala is the envoy; antagonised by Scrophularia (玄參) and snake slough.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE — the classical form is a WINE, not a tea: 「造酒之方，用五加根皮洗淨去骨，莖葉亦可，以水煎汁，和麴釀米酒成，時時飲之」 (Li Shizhen, 發明, BCGM 1596); 「釀酒飲，治風痺四肢攣急」 (Su Song). 王綸 in the same passage: 「風病飲酒能生痰火，惟五加一味浸酒，日飲數盃，最有益」. Wu Yiluo 1757 repeats 「酿酒尤良」.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS (本經, via BCGM 1596): 心腹疝氣、腹痛、益氣療躄、小兒三歲不能行、疽瘡陰蝕. 別錄 adds 男子陰痿、囊下濕、小便餘瀝、女人陰癢及腰脊痛、兩腳疼痺、風弱五緩虛羸、補中益精、堅筋骨、強志意、久服輕身耐老. Note this is a WIND-DAMP / musculoskeletal drug in the classical idiom, plus a paediatric delayed-walking remedy — NOT the 'chronic stress with depletion, nervous/immune/endocrine' profile stored in the database, which is 20th-century Soviet adaptogen research reasoning.

DB CITATION IS FABRICATED — FLAG FOR REMOVAL. The stored primary_text_citation excerpt reads 'Wu Jia Pi … said to warm the spleen-qi, replenish wei (defensive) qi, and restore the patient suffering from fatigue, cold limbs, and weakened spirit' with locator 'warms the qi, builds the will, lengthens the years'. NONE of that is in the Shennong text. The actual Shennong entry is 主心腹疝氣，腹痛，益氣療躄，小兒不能行，疸創陰蝕. There is no spleen-qi, no wei-qi, no cold limbs, no weakened spirit. The URL (archive.org/details/shennong-bencao-jing, dated '1892') does not correspond to a verifiable pre-1900 edition.

results.pre1900_finding: For the SEED KERNEL, not the leaf: 甘苦平濇無毒 — sweet and bitter, NEUTRAL, astringent, non-toxic (raw), with Li Shizhen adding that COOKED it becomes 性溫、有小毒 (slightly warm, slightly toxic). results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目, 1596, Siku Quanshu recension, 卷30 果部, entry 銀杏 (釋名 白果、鴨脚子): 「核仁氣味甘苦平濇無毒」，「時珍曰：熟食小苦㣲甘，性温，有小毒，多食令人臚脹。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷30 . 發明: 「時珍曰：銀杏宋初始著名，而修本草者不收…其氣薄味厚，性濇而收，色白屬金，故能入肺經，益肺氣，定喘嗽，縮小便。」 Wu Yiluo 吳儀洛, 本草從新, 1757, 卷十果部, 銀杏: 「甘苦收濇。熟食溫肺益氣…生食降浊痰，解酒消毒，殺虫。」 https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: NONE. Ginkgo is NOT in the Shennong Bencao Jing. Li Shizhen says so explicitly: 「銀杏宋初始著名，而修本草者不收」 — it only became known in the early Song and earlier materia-medica compilers did not include it. Its BCGM source-tag is 「日用」 (Riyong Bencao, Yuan dynasty), not 本經. There is therefore no upper/middle/lower grade and no ancient warrant for prolonged daily use.

PART DISCIPLINE — THIS IS THE HEADLINE. BCGM 1596 卷30 gives an assignment for 核仁 (the kernel/nut) ONLY. There is no 葉 (leaf) section in the Siku recension of the entry. Every pre-1900 statement about ginkgo's temperature, actions and toxicity is about the NUT. The database row is for the LEAF. The leaf preparation is a 20th-century European development and cannot be back-dated onto Li Shizhen.

CHANNEL ENTRY 歸經: 「色白屬金，故能入肺經」 (Li Shizhen, BCGM 1596) — LUNG channel, reasoned from the white colour/Metal phase. Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757 repeats it verbatim: 「色白屬金，故入肺。」 Note the database stores tcm_pattern_match as 'Blood Stasis, Kidney Essence Deficiency affecting Brain' — a modern cerebrovascular reading with NO pre-1900 support whatsoever. Li Shizhen's ginkgo is a LUNG and BLADDER drug.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS (BCGM 1596): 熟食溫肺益氣、定喘嗽、縮小便、止白濁；生食降痰、消毒、殺蟲、嚼漿塗鼻面手足去皶皰. Cooked it warms the lung, settles panting cough, reduces urinary frequency, stops turbid discharge; raw it descends phlegm and kills worms, and the pulp is rubbed on the face for acne.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE — RAW vs COOKED CHANGES THE DRUG. Raw = 平 (neutral) and descending/detoxifying; cooked = 溫 (warm) with 小毒 and lung-warming. This is a genuine thermal split inside one plant part and the database has no way to represent it.

CONTRAINDICATION / TOXICITY, stated in the strongest terms in the source: 「然食多則收令太過，令人氣壅臚脹昏頓」 and 「三元延壽書言：白果食滿千箇者死。又云：昔有飢者同以白果代飯，食飽，次日皆死也」 (BCGM 1596, 發明). Also 呉瑞: 「多食壅氣動風，小兒多食昏霍發驚引疳，同鰻鱺魚食患軟風」 — children especially, and an explicit food incompatibility with eel. Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757: 「多食則收濇太過，令人壅氣胪胀，小兒發驚动疳。」 A pre-1900 lethal-dose report and a paediatric warning belong in any product record.

DB CITATION IS FABRICATED — FLAG FOR REMOVAL. The stored primary_text_citation excerpt reads 'Yin Xing … is described as astringent and warming, used for chronic cough with phlegm in the aged, and for involuntary urination from kidney-yang deficiency', titled 'Bencao Gangmu — pre-1928 English partial translations', URL https://ctext.org/wiki.pl?if=en&res=635617. BCGM says 平 (neutral), not warming, for the raw kernel; there is no 'kidney-yang deficiency' language in the entry (the mechanism given is 入肺經); and ctext.org is CAPTCHA-gated so no text could have been read at that URL. The stored secondary is ESCOP 2019, forbidden.

results.pre1900_finding: 甘微寒 — sweet, SLIGHTLY COLD. Both the Han-dynasty layer and Li Shizhen's head-reading make ginseng root slightly COLD, not warm. But the assignment is genuinely contested in the pre-1900 record and is preparation-dependent: 別錄 says 微溫, Wu Yiluo 1757 says 甘溫, and Li Yanwen (quoted by Li Shizhen) resolves it as 「人參生用氣涼，熟用氣温」 — RAW it is cool, PROCESSED/COOKED it is warm. The stored 'Warm' is defensible only for the cooked/red-processed root and flatly contradicts the 本經/綱目 head-reading for the raw root. Do not collapse this to one value.
results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目, 1596, Siku Quanshu recension, 卷12上, entry 人參 (headed 「人參」{{本經上品}}): 「根氣味甘微寒無毒」，note: 「别録曰㣲温；普曰神農小寒，桐君、雷公苦，黄帝、岐伯甘無毒；元素曰性温，味甘微苦，氣味俱薄，浮而升，陽中之陽也。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷12上 . 發明: 「言聞曰：人參生用氣涼，熟用氣温；味甘補陽，微苦補隂。」 ANCIENT LAYER: 神農本草經, Sun Xingyan 孫星衍 recension, 1799, 卷一·上經: 「人參　味甘，微寒。主補五臟，安精神，定魂魄，止驚悸，除邪氣，明目、開心、益智。久服，輕身、延年。一名人銜，一名鬼蓋。生山谷。」 with the 吳普 variant readings preserved: 「神農：甘，小寒；桐君、雷公：苦；岐伯、黃帝：甘，無毒；扁鵲：有毒。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw . DISSENTING 18th-CENTURY READING: Wu Yiluo 吳儀洛, 本草從新, 1757: 「人參…甘溫微苦。大補肺中元氣。」 https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 (upper grade) — 「本經上品」 in BCGM 1596, and located in 卷一·上經 of the 1799 recension. Upper grade, 久服輕身延年 — explicitly sanctioned for prolonged use.

THE CONTRADICTION IS ANCIENT AND SHOULD BE PUBLISHED, NOT RESOLVED. The 1799 Sun Xingyan recension preserves four named authorities disagreeing inside the Han text itself: Shennong 甘小寒 (sweet, mildly cold), Tongjun & Leigong 苦 (bitter), Qibo & Huangdi 甘無毒, and Bianque 有毒 (TOXIC). One of the four ancient authorities called ginseng toxic. That is a fact about the tradition that a 'temperature: Warm' cell erases.

PART DISCIPLINE — THE RHIZOME HEAD IS A DIFFERENT DRUG WITH THE OPPOSITE ACTION: 「蘆氣味苦温無毒。主治吐虚勞痰飲」 (BCGM 1596 卷12上). The 蘆 (reed-head/rhizome neck) is bitter and WARM and is an EMETIC. 「震亨曰：人參入手太隂，補陽中之隂；蘆則反能瀉太隂之陽」 — the root supplements, the head drains. If a product uses whole root with the neck left on, it is not the same drug.

CHANNEL ENTRY 歸經: 手太陰 (Hand Taiyin / LUNG) — 「震亨曰：人參入手大隂」 (Zhu Zhenheng, BCGM 1596). Zhang Yuansu adds routing pairs: 「人參得升麻，引用補上焦之元氣，瀉肺中之火；得茯苓，引用補下焦之元氣，瀉腎中之火；得麥門冬則生脉；得乾薑則補氣。」 The channel destination is set by the PARTNER HERB. Database stores 'Kidney Yang Deficiency, Spleen Qi Deficiency' — the classical head is LUNG.

INCOMPATIBILITIES, explicit and severe: 「之才曰：茯苓、馬藺為之使；惡溲疏、鹵鹹；反藜蘆；一云畏五靈脂，惡皂莢、黑豆，動紫石英」 (BCGM 1596). And Zhu Zhenheng: 「人參…與藜蘆相反，服參一兩，入藜蘆一錢，其功盡廢也」 — one qian of Veratrum destroys one liang of ginseng. This 十八反 pairing is a hard formulation rule with no database column.

CONTRAINDICATIONS, stated in the 正誤 (errata) section of BCGM 1596 — the strongest classical warnings: 「斆曰：夏月少使人參，發心痃之病」; 「王綸曰：凡酒色過度，損傷肺腎真陰，陰虛火動，勞嗽吐血、欬血等證，勿用之…若誤用參耆甘温之劑，則病日增，服之過多則死，不可治。」 Do not use in yin-vacuity with stirring fire, blood-spitting cough — misuse is said to be fatal. Wu Yiluo 1757 adds: 「肺有火熱及肺氣不利者忌之。表有邪者忌之。凡痧痘斑毒欲出未出…若誤用之，以阻截其路，為祸尤烈。」 Contraindicated when an exterior pathogen is present or a rash is trying to erupt.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE: 「凡生用宜㕮咀，熟用宜隔紙焙之，或醇酒潤透㕮咀焙熟用，並忌鐡器」 (Li Yanwen, 修治, BCGM 1596). Never iron vessels. Storage doctrine too: 「人參易蛀蚛，惟納新器中宻封可經年不壊」 and store interleaved with 華陰細辛. And the therapeutic split: 「土虚火旺之病，則宜生參涼薄之氣以瀉火而補土…脾虚肺怯之病，則宜熟參甘温之味以補土而生金」 — raw ginseng for vacuity-fire, cooked ginseng for spleen/lung weakness.

SPECIES/TRADE NOTE: Wu Yiluo 1757 already distinguishes 東洋 and 西洋 ginseng in commerce and separately grades 參條, 參須, 太子參, 參蘆, 珠兒參, 黨參 — and says of the LEAF: 「參葉大苦大寒，損氣败血，其性與人參相反」 (leaf is very bitter, very COLD, and acts opposite to the root). Part discipline again.

The BCGM mushroom section 卷28 菜之五 芝栭類 lists exactly fifteen fungi — 芝、木耳、杉菌、皁角蕈、香蕈、葛花菜、天花蕈、蘑菰蕈、雞㙡、舵菜、土菌、竹蓐、雚菌、地耳、石耳 — and 猴頭 is not among them. The strings 猴頭, 㺅頭 and 猴菇 occur ZERO times in every BCGM volume downloaded (卷12上, 18上, 27, 28, 29, 30, 36, 37) and zero times in Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757 (177,032 characters).

THE STORED CITATION IS FABRICATED AND MUST BE DELETED. primary_text_citation claims Wu Qijun 吳其濬, 植物名實圖考 (1848), with the 'excerpt': 'Hou Tou Gu is recorded among the medicinal fungi of Northeastern China; described as sweet, neutral, tonifying to the spleen-qi and the stomach; particularly indicated where digestive weakness coexists with mental fatigue.' Three independent problems: (a) the URL is https://ctext.org/wiki.pl?if=en&res=541547 and ctext.org serves a CAPTCHA interstitial to automated access and returns ERR_REQUIRES_AUTHENTICATION on its API, so no text could have been read there; (b) Zhiwu Mingshi Tukao is a botanical identification work and no full text of it is reachable at all (Wikisource has only the volume tables of contents proofread; archive.org has no scan) — it is UNTESTED, so nothing can be quoted from it either way; (c) the quoted English is in the register of a modern TCM website, not of an 1848 Chinese botanical treatise, and the specific claim 'sweet, neutral' is precisely the stored database value, which is the signature of a citation written to justify a value rather than a value read out of a citation.

SECOND FABRICATION IN THE SAME ROW: the stored energetics claim 'Kidney Essence Deficiency, Heart-Spleen Qi Deficiency' and 'Vata (cognitive deficiency)' have no pre-1900 warrant of any kind. Hericium's nootropic reputation rests entirely on Japanese NGF research from the 1990s onward.

RECOMMENDATION: mark this row 'no classical energetics; modern attribution only' rather than carrying 'Neutral' forward with a citation attached. If the product needs a temperature for the matcher, it must be flagged as an EDITORIAL assignment by Eden, not as a classical one.

results.pre1900_finding: 赤芝 (red zhi = Ganoderma lucidum) is 苦平 — BITTER, NEUTRAL, non-toxic. Not warm. The 'warm' reading in circulation belongs to a DIFFERENT zhi: 紫芝 (purple zhi, Ganoderma sinense) is 甘溫, and even there Zhen Quan dissented with 平. The pre-1900 texts assign each of the six zhi its own flavour and all six are 平 except 紫芝: 青芝 酸平, 赤芝 苦平, 黃芝 甘平, 白芝 辛平, 黑芝 鹹平, 紫芝 甘溫. Stored 'Warm' with taste 'Bitter, Sweet' looks like 赤芝 and 紫芝 fused into one row.
results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目, 1596, Siku Quanshu recension, 卷28 菜之五 芝栭類, entry 芝 (headed 「芝」{{本經上品}}，校正：併入本經青赤黄白黒紫六芝): 「赤芝一名丹芝（本經）氣味苦平無毒。主治胸中結，益心氣，補中，増智慧，不忘。久食輕身不老延年神仙（本經）。」 and, for contrast, 「紫芝一名木芝（本經）氣味甘温無毒（甄權曰平）。主治耳聾，利闗節，保神，益精氣，堅筋骨，好顔色。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷28 . ANCIENT LAYER, independently confirming: 神農本草經, Sun Xingyan 孫星衍 recension, 1799, 卷一·上經: 「赤芝　味苦，平。主胸中結，益心氣，補中，增智慧，不忘。久食，輕身、不老、延年、神仙。一名丹芝。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 (upper grade) — 「芝」{{本經上品}} in BCGM 1596 卷28; all six zhi sit in 卷一·上經 of the 1799 recension, and the 名醫 note there states 「六芝皆無毒，六月、八月采」. Upper grade, explicitly non-toxic, explicitly for long-term use (久食). This is the strongest classical warrant for daily use of any herb in this batch.

THE SIX-ZHI TABLE, all from BCGM 1596 卷28 — the database collapses six distinct drugs into one row: 青芝（龍芝）酸平，主明目、補肝氣、安精魂、仁恕；赤芝（丹芝）苦平，主胸中結、益心氣、補中、增智慧、不忘；黃芝（金芝）甘平，主心腹五邪、益脾氣、安神、忠信和樂；白芝（玉芝／素芝）辛平，主欬逆上氣、益肺氣、通利口鼻、強志意、安魄；黑芝（玄芝）鹹平，主利水道、益腎氣、通九竅、聰察；紫芝（木芝）甘溫，主耳聾、利關節、保神、益精氣、堅筋骨、好顏色. Five colours, five zang, five flavours — an explicit five-phase organ assignment scheme. Ganoderma lucidum = 赤芝 = HEART. Ganoderma sinense = 紫芝.

INCOMPATIBILITIES / ENVOY, applying to all six: 「之才曰：青、赤、黄、白、黒、紫六芝，並以薯蕷為之使，得髪良，得蔴子仁、白瓜子、牡桂甚益人，惡常山，畏扁青、茵蔯蒿。」 (Xu Zhicai, in BCGM 1596). Chinese yam (薯蕷) is the envoy; antagonised by Dichroa (常山); fears azurite (扁青) and Artemisia capillaris (茵蔯蒿). NOTE: in the Wikisource transcription 白瓜子 is printed 白{{SKchar|2201}}子 with a lacuna glyph — verify against a clean scan before publishing that term.
CHANNEL ENTRY 歸經: none given in BCGM 1596. The organ targeting is expressed through the five-colour/five-zang scheme above (赤芝 → 心, heart-qi) rather than as a 歸經 formula.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS for the red zhi specifically, in the source's own idiom: 胸中結 (bindings/knotting in the chest), 益心氣 (boosts heart qi), 補中 (supplements the centre), 増智慧、不忘 (increases wisdom, prevents forgetting). The database's 'Heart Shen disturbance' is reasonable; 'Kidney Qi and Essence Deficiency' and 'Wei Qi Deficiency' are not in the classical entry — the essence/bone claims (益精氣、堅筋骨) belong to 紫芝.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE and a candour note from Li Shizhen himself: 陶弘景 records 「凡得芝草便正爾食之，無餘節度，故皆不云服法也」 — no processing regimen was ever transmitted, it was simply eaten. Li Shizhen then adds a remarkable sceptical passage: 「時珍嘗疑芝乃腐朽餘氣所生，正如人生瘤贅，而古今皆以為瑞草，又云服食可仙，誠為迂謬」 — he suspected zhi is just decay-growth like a wart, and called the immortality claims absurd. He also reports 「方士以木積濕處，用藥傅之，即生五色芝」 — that alchemists FAKED five-colour zhi by treating damp wood, and one such fake was presented to the Jiajing Emperor. A 1596 fraud warning on this exact commodity.
CAUTION ON THE NAME 靈芝: in BCGM 1596 卷28 the term 靈芝 is used as an alias for 石耳 (rock-ear lichen), not for Ganoderma — 「石耳…釋名靈芝（靈苑方）氣味甘平無毒」. Searching classical texts for 靈芝 will pull the wrong drug.

DB CITATION PROBLEM: the stored primary_text_citation excerpt ('The Six Zhi … are described as tonics for the heart-qi and the shen; relieve internal-organ accumulations') is a paraphrase, not a quote, with URL archive.org/details/shennong-bencao-jing dated '1892' — no verifiable pre-1900 edition. The stored secondary is a 2011 NCBI bookshelf chapter, forbidden.

results.pre1900_finding: 酸溫 — sour, WARM, non-toxic. Confirmed in the Han layer (1799 Sun Xingyan recension of the Shennong canon), in Li Shizhen 1596, and again in Wu Yiluo 1757 (性溫). But the pre-1900 record also preserves a named dissent: Kou Zongshi observed 「本經言其性温，今食之多致虛熱，小兒益甚」 — the canon calls it warm, yet eating much of it produces vacuity heat, especially in children.
results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目, 1596, Siku Quanshu recension, 卷18上 草部蔓草類, entry 五味子 (headed 「五味子」{{本經上品}}): 「氣味酸温無毒」，note: 「好古曰：味酸微苦鹹，味厚氣輕，隂中微陽，入手太隂血分、足少隂氣分。時珍曰：酸鹹入肝而補腎，辛苦入心而補肺，甘入中宫益脾胃。之才曰：蓯蓉為之使，惡萎㽔，勝烏頭。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷18上 . ANCIENT LAYER: 神農本草經, Sun Xingyan 孫星衍 recension, 1799, 卷一·上經: 「五味子　味酸，溫。主益氣，咳逆上氣，勞傷羸瘦。補不足，強陰，益男子精。生山谷。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw . 18th-CENTURY CONFIRMATION: Wu Yiluo 吳儀洛, 本草從新, 1757: 「五味子…性溫。五味俱備。（皮甘、肉酸、核中苦辛、都有鹹味、酸鹹爲多。）」
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 (upper grade) — 「本經上品」 in BCGM 1596 卷18上, and located in 卷一·上經 of the 1799 recension. Sanctioned for prolonged use.

CHANNEL ENTRY 歸經: 「入手太隂血分、足少隂氣分」 — Wang Haogu, quoted in BCGM 1596. Hand Taiyin (LUNG) BLOOD division and Foot Shaoyin (KIDNEY) QI division. Note the crossover: lung via blood, kidney via qi. That precision is exactly what the database has no room for. CAUTION: the Wikisource transcription of 本草從新 1757 renders the same Wang Haogu line as 「入手太陽血分、足少陰氣分」 (Taiyang, not Taiyin) — a transcription divergence between the two texts. Quote the BCGM traditional text.

FIVE-FLAVOUR DOCTRINE, and the classical justification of the name: 「恭曰：五味，皮肉甘酸，核中辛苦，都有鹹味，此則五味其也。本經但云味酸，當以木為五行之先也」 (Su Gong, in BCGM 1596) — the skin and flesh are sweet-sour, the kernel acrid-bitter, and the whole carries salt; the canon lists only 'sour' because Wood leads the five phases. Li Shizhen then maps flavour to organ: 「酸鹹入肝而補腎，辛苦入心而補肺，甘入中宫益脾胃」 — ONE berry reaching all five zang by five different flavours. The database's 'All doshas (balancing)' is a rough analogue of a doctrine that is stated far more precisely in the source.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, explicit and two-branched: 「斆曰：凡用以銅刀劈作兩片，用蜜浸蒸，從已至申，却以漿浸一宿，焙乾用」 — split with a BRONZE knife (not iron), honey-soaked and steamed from si to shen hour, then soaked overnight in fermented millet water and dried. And the split: 「時珍曰：入補藥熟用，入嗽藥生用」 — PROCESSED for tonic use, RAW for cough. Wu Yiluo 1757 repeats: 「入滋補藥，每粒銅刀切作两片，蜜酒拌蒸，晒乾焙…入劳嗽藥，捶碎核，生用。」 A product that uses one preparation for both purposes is departing from stated doctrine.

CONTRAINDICATION, stated repeatedly: 「杲曰：…但有外邪者不可驟用，恐閉其邪氣，必先發散而後用之乃良」 (Li Gao, BCGM 1596) — must NOT be given abruptly where an exterior pathogen is present; it would lock the pathogen in. Wu Yiluo 1757 is blunter: 「唯風邪在表、痧疹初發、一切停飲、肺家有實熱者，皆當禁之。」 Forbidden in exterior wind, at the onset of rash, in fluid retention, and in lung repletion-heat.

THE DISSENT, worth publishing: 「宗奭曰：…本經言其性温，今食之多致虛熱，小兒益甚。藥性論謂其除熱氣，日華子謂其暖水臟除煩熱，後學至此多惑」 (Kou Zongshi, in BCGM 1596). Zhu Zhenheng then argues the objection away: 「寇氏所謂食之多致虚熱者，葢收補之驟也」. A 1596 text printing both sides of a temperature dispute is the ideal model for how Eden should represent contested values.
INCOMPATIBILITIES: 「蓯蓉為之使，惡萎㽔，勝烏頭」 (Xu Zhicai, in BCGM 1596) — Cistanche is the envoy; antagonised by Polygonatum odoratum (葳蕤); overcomes/masters aconite (烏頭). Wu Yiluo 1757 repeats 「苁蓉爲使，惡葳蕤。」

SOURCING, and it changes the indication: 「時珍曰：五味今有南北之分，南産者色紅，北産者色黑，入滋補藥必用北産者乃良」 and 汪機: 「生津止渴、潤肺補腎、勞嗽宜用北者；風寒在肺宜用南者。」 Northern (black) for tonification, southern (red) for wind-cold in the lung. Two commodities, two uses, one name.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS (本經, via BCGM 1596): 益氣、欬逆上氣、勞傷羸瘦、補不足、強陰、益男子精. 別錄 adds 養五臟、除熱、生陰中肌. A pre-1900 preparation of note: Sun Simiao's summer tonic — 「五六月宜常服五味子湯，以益肺金之氣，在上則滋源，在下則補腎…以五味子一大合，木臼搗細，甕瓶中以百沸湯投之，入少蜜封，置火邊良久湯成，任飲」 — a seasonal (5th-6th month) honey infusion, not a decoction.

results.pre1900_finding: No pre-1900 source assigns ANY thermal quality to Boswellia serrata. All four standard pre-1900 authorities that treat the tree (Ainslie 1826, Dutt 1877, Watt 1889, Dymock 1890) record taste, provenance and use only. Two of them state outright that whatever Sanskrit doctrine exists attaches to imported Arabian olibanum, not to the Indian tree. Stored 'Warm' is therefore unsupported by any admissible source, in either direction.
results.source_year: 1826 / 1877 / 1889 / 1890 — all pre-1900, none assigns a temperature
results.evidence: Sir George Watt, A Dictionary of the Economic Products of India, Vol. I, Calcutta, 1889, p.516 (Boswellia serrata): "Very little of a definite nature is known of the medicinal virtues of this gum. It is probable that all that has been written on the subject should be considered as applying exclusively to imported Olibanum." Same page: "The Sanskrit name Kunduru, derived from the Arabic word Kundur, is most probably wrongly applied to the gum-resin of this species. It should be restricted to frankincense, a substance which reaches India from Arabia and Africa. The true Sanskrit name for this plant is most probably Sallaki, from which is derived the Hindi word Salai." URL https://archive.org/download/lbg.381.025954.wat.6106/lbg.381.025954.wat.6106_djvu.txt (line 52735ff). — U. C. Dutt, The Materia Medica of the Hindus, Calcutta, 1877, pp.135-136, entire entry: "OLIBANUM. The gum of the Salai tree of India (Boswellia thurifera), is called Kunduru in Sanskrit. It is used as an incense and as a local application to buboes." No quality assigned. URL https://archive.org/download/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft_djvu.txt — Whitelaw Ainslie, Materia Indica, Vol. I, London, 1826, p.266: "its Sanscrit name is sallaci, in Hindoostanie it is called salai" — botanical and commercial description only, no quality. URL https://archive.org/download/materiaindicaors01ains/materiaindicaors01ains_djvu.txt — Dymock, Warden & Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. I, 1890, p.302 (Boswellia serrata): the history "is involved in much obscurity, owing to its having been confounded by both native and European writers with true Frankincense and Bdellium." URL https://archive.org/download/mobot31753000263365/mobot31753000263365_djvu.txt
additions: SPECIES TRAP, CONFIRMED BY THE SOURCES THEMSELVES. The material that DOES carry a classical thermal assignment is Arabian frankincense (Boswellia sacra/carterii), not B. serrata. Bencao Gangmu 卷34 薫陸香乳香 (Li Shizhen, 1596) reads 「氣味微温無毒」with the dissent 「大明曰乳香辛熱微毒；元素曰苦辛純陽」— slightly warm and non-toxic in the head line, pungent-hot and slightly toxic per Da Ming, bitter-pungent pure-yang per Zhang Yuansu. That entry's own 集解 places the drug in 大食國 (Arabia), 波斯 (Persia) and 天竺. Do NOT carry this across to a B. serrata monograph. URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷34&action=raw

GRADE, for the Chinese analogue only: 薫陸香乳香 is headed 「别録上品」 — upper grade of the Mingyi Bielu, not of the Shennong Bencao Jing. B. serrata itself has no Chinese entry and therefore no Shennong grade at all.

CHANNEL ENTRY (归经), for the Chinese analogue only: 本草從新 (吳儀洛, 1757) 乳香: 「苦溫。辛香善窜。入心。通行十二經。」 — enters the Heart, travels through all twelve channels. URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS for Salai gugul as actually recorded pre-1900 (Watt 1889, Vol I p.516): "used in rheumatism, nervous diseases, scrofulous affections, urinary disorders, and skin diseases, and is generally combined with aromatics. It is regarded as a diaphoretic and astringent, and is used in the preparation of ointment for sores." Also: prescribed with clarified butter in syphilitic disease; with cocoanut oil for sores; as a stimulant in pulmonary disease; mixed with gum acacia as a corrective for foul breath. Dutt 1877: incense, and local application to buboes.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, Chinese analogue (BCGM 卷34 修治, 1596): 「入丸散微炒殺毒則不粘」 — for pills and powders it must be lightly dry-fried, which kills its toxicity and stops it sticking; grind it in a mortar standing in hot water, or with lampwick or a few grains of glutinous rice, to get it fine.
CONTRAINDICATION, Chinese analogue (本草從新, 1757): 「瘡疽已溃勿服。脓多勿敷。」 — do not give internally once an abscess has already ulcerated; do not apply it where there is copious pus.

DATABASE INTEGRITY FLAG. The stored primary_text_citation for H084 quotes a long passage attributed to the Sushruta Samhita via K. K. L. Bhishagratna's English translation, asserting Shallaki is "cooling-to-neutral" in virya. That translation is 1907-16, i.e. inadmissible under the pre-1900 rule, and I could not locate the quoted passage in any accessible text. It should be treated as unverified pending sight of the Sanskrit original. The stored secondary (WHO Monographs Vol. 4, 2009) is also post-1900.

results.pre1900_finding: Warm, unanimously and across seventeen centuries. Shennong Bencao Jing: 味甘，溫 (sweet, warm). Bencao Gangmu head line: 氣味苦温無毒 (bitter, warm, non-toxic), with the Mingyi Bielu reading 辛大温 (pungent, GREATLY warm). Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757: 甘溫…辛溫…苦溫. The only variation is in the TASTE, which is contested (sweet / bitter / pungent), never in the temperature.
results.source_year: 1596 (Bencao Gangmu); corroborated 1799 recension of c. 200 CE text and 1757
results.evidence: 本草綱目 卷14 當歸 (李時珍, 1596): 「氣味苦温無毒」…「别錄曰辛大温，普曰神農黄帝桐君扁鵲甘無毒，岐伯雷公辛無毒，李當之小温，杲曰甘辛温無毒，氣厚味薄，可升可降，陽中微隂，入手少隂足太隂厥隂經血分」. URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷14&action=raw — 神農本草經, 孫星衍・孫馮翼輯本, 1799 (recension of the c. 200 CE original): 「當歸 味甘，溫。主咳逆上氣，溫瘧、寒熱，洗在皮膚中，婦人漏下絕子，諸惡創瘍、金創。煮飲之。一名干歸。生川谷。《吳普》曰：當歸，神農、黃帝、桐君、扁鵲：甘，無毒；岐伯、雷公：辛，無毒；李氏：小溫。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw — 本草從新 (吳儀洛, 1757): 「當歸…甘溫和血。辛溫散内寒。苦溫助心散寒。入心肝脾…爲血中氣藥。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 中品 MIDDLE grade. BCGM heads the entry 「本經中品」, and Sun Xingyan's 1799 recension lists 當歸 in the 草，中品 index. This is directly load-bearing for a product recommending daily herbs: the Bencao Jing's three-grade system encodes intended duration, and middle-grade substances are explicitly NOT the indefinite-daily class that upper-grade herbs are. Dang Gui carries no 久服輕身 formula, unlike Chai Hu and Di Huang in this same batch.

CHANNEL ENTRY (归经): 「入手少隂足太隂厥隂經血分」 (李杲, in BCGM 1596) — Hand Shaoyin (Heart), Foot Taiyin (Spleen), Foot Jueyin (Liver), at the BLOOD level specifically. 本草從新 1757 restates: 「入心肝脾。（心生血、肝藏血、脾統血。）爲血中氣藥」 — the Heart engenders blood, the Liver stores it, the Spleen governs it; Dang Gui is 'the qi-medicine within the blood'.

PART DOCTRINE — the single largest gap in the stored row. Head, body, tail and whole root are four different medicines. BCGM 卷14 根修治, quoting 張元素: 「頭止血，尾破血，身和血，全用即一破一止也」 (head stops blood, tail breaks blood, body harmonises blood, the whole does both at once). 李杲: 「頭止血而上行，身養血而中守，梢破血而下流，全活血而不走」. Li Shizhen adjudicates for Zhang Yuansu: 「治上當用頭，治中當用身，治下當用尾，通治則全用」. A single 'Dong Quai' row with one temperature and one action set flattens a four-way distinction the classical texts treat as decisive.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE: 「凡用去蘆頭，以酒浸一宿」 — remove the crown and steep in wine overnight (雷斆, BCGM). 「治上酒浸，治外酒洗」 — wine-steeped to treat the upper body, wine-washed to treat the exterior (張元素). 本草從新 1757: 「宜酒制。治吐血。宜醋炒」 — wine-processed as standard, vinegar-fried for blood-vomiting. Storage: 「凡晒乾乗熱紙封甕收之，不蛀」 — sun-dry, wrap in paper while still warm, seal in a jar, and it will not worm.

PROVENANCE DOCTRINE (a sourcing rule with no DB column): 韓懋, in BCGM 1596: 「川産者力剛而善攻，秦産者力柔而善補」 — Sichuan-grown is forceful and attacks; Qin-grown is gentle and supplements. Repeated verbatim in 本草從新 1757: 「川產力剛善攻。秦產力柔善補。」 The two are not interchangeable.

CONTRAINDICATIONS AS STATED CLASSICALLY: BCGM 1596, 之才: 「惡䕡茹、濕麫；畏菖蒲、海藻、牡蒙；生薑制雄黄」. 本草從新 1757 adds a hard clinical one the DB entirely lacks: 「极善滑腸。瀉者禁用。」 — extremely apt to loosen the bowel; FORBIDDEN in anyone with diarrhoea. Also 「畏菖蒲、海藻、生薑。惡溼面。」

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the Bencao Jing's own idiom (1799 recension of c. 200 CE): 「主咳逆上氣，溫瘧、寒熱，洗在皮膚中，婦人漏下絕子，諸惡創瘍、金創。煮飲之。」 — cough with counterflow qi rising; warm-malaria with chills and fever; a skin condition; women's leaking discharge and infertility; all malignant sores and metal wounds; taken as a decoction. Note that the ancient indication list is led by a RESPIRATORY complaint, not a gynaecological one — Wang Haogu addresses this puzzle directly in BCGM: 「當歸其味辛散，乃血中氣藥也…欬逆上氣有隂虛陽無所附者，故用血藥補隂則血和而氣降矣」.

FORMULA CONTEXT (no DB field): 「古方四物湯以為君，芍藥為臣，地黄為佐，芎藭為使」 (韓懋, BCGM 1596) — Dang Gui is sovereign in Si Wu Tang, with Bai Shao as minister, Di Huang as assistant, Chuan Xiong as envoy. Note that H104 in this same batch is the assistant in that pair.
SPECIES: 當歸 = Angelica sinensis throughout. Not Angelica archangelica. BCGM's 卷13 lists a separate 土當歸 ('earth dang gui') as a distinct drug — do not conflate.

results.pre1900_finding: The pre-1900 record for Gymnema sylvestre gives RASA and ACTIONS but no virya. Dymock transmits Madanapala's Nighantu as "a pungent taste and the properties of an astringent and bitter stomachic" — a taste and two action words, none of which is a thermal assignment. Watt 1890 gives snake-bite use and the sweet-suppression phenomenon and no quality at all. Dutt 1877 carries Meshasringi only in his Sanskrit-name glossary, with no monograph. Stored 'Cool' has no admissible support.
results.source_year: 1877 / 1890 / 1890-93 — all pre-1900, none assigns a virya
results.evidence: Dymock, Warden & Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. II, pp.450-451 (Gymnema sylvestre): "This shrubby climbing plant is called Meshasringi, 'ram's horn,' in Sanskrit, but it is not mentioned in the Raja Nirghanta. It is considered to be the Meshasringi of Madanpal's Nighanta and of the Marathi and Guzerathi Nighantas, which are little more than translations of that work. It bears the following synonyms — Mesha vishanika, Meshavalli, Sarpa-darushtrika, Anyada, Kshina-vartta, Vrikshikali and Vishanika, and is described as having a pungent taste and the properties of an astringent and bitter stomachic; useful in cough, biliousness, boils, sore eyes." URL https://archive.org/download/mobot31753000263373/mobot31753000263373_djvu.txt (line 22703ff). — Sir George Watt, A Dictionary of the Economic Products of India, Vol. IV, Calcutta, 1890, s.v. Gymnema sylvestre: the whole Medicine paragraph is snake-bite use plus the Edgeworth/Hooper taste experiments; no quality of any kind is assigned. URL https://archive.org/download/in.ernet.dli.2015.83717/in.ernet.dli.2015.83717_djvu.txt (line 22105ff). — U. C. Dutt, Materia Medica of the Hindus, 1877: 'Meshasringi / Merisingi, B. H. / Gymnema sylvestre, R. Br. / Syn. Asclepias geminata, Roxb.' appears ONLY in the Sanskrit glossary; there is no monograph and no properties. URL https://archive.org/download/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft_djvu.txt (line 15489ff).
additions: NEGATIVE BIBLIOGRAPHIC FACT WORTH STORING: Dymock states the plant "is not mentioned in the Raja Nirghanta", and Dutt 1877 gives it no monograph. Gymnema has a thin classical footprint — it is a Madanapala-and-later herb, not a Charaka/Sushruta-tier one. That should temper how confidently the product asserts Ayurvedic energetics for it.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the source's own idiom (Madanapala's Nighantu via Dymock, Vol. II): "useful in cough, biliousness, boils, sore eyes." Note 'biliousness' = the Pitta-derangement idiom of the Anglo-Indian translators.

SNAKE-BITE DOCTRINE, the herb's dominant pre-1900 use, entirely absent from the DB: "It is also in repute amongst the Hindus as a remedy for snake bite, the powdered root being applied to the part bitten, and a decoction administered internally" (Dymock, Vol. II). Watt 1890 opens his Medicine paragraph the same way: "The root has long been esteemed amongst the Hindus as a remedy for snake bite." The PART is the ROOT, not the leaf the DB stores.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE (Dymock, Vol. II, Konkan practice): "the dried and powdered leaf is used as an errhine, and the fresh leaves crushed and mixed with water, as a cooling bath for children in the hot weather." Errhine = snuff, i.e. a nasal route the DB does not record. NOTE: the 'cooling bath' is a use, not a virya, and must not be counted as a thermal assignment.

SANSKRIT SYNONYMS recorded pre-1900 (Dymock, Vol. II): Meshasringi ('ram's horn'), Mesha vishanika, Meshavalli, Sarpa-darushtrika, Anyada, Kshina-vartta, Vrikshikali, Vishanika. Sarpa-darushtrika encodes the snake-bite use in the name itself.

TASTE — the pre-1900 sources disagree with the DB. Dymock's own Description of the leaf: "taste saltish and acrid." The nighantu reading he transmits is "pungent." The DB stores 'bitter, astringent'. Neither pre-1900 reading is bitter-astringent as the primary rasa. Flag for founder decision.

THE SWEET-SUPPRESSION PROPERTY IS PRE-1900 AND WELL DOCUMENTED, so the DB's headline claim is safe: first noted by Edgeworth, tested by D. Hooper in 1887 and reported in Dymock Vol. II — "After chewing one or two leaves it was proved undoubtedly that sugar had no taste immediately afterwards." Hooper also found it abolishes BITTER: quinine sulphate "taken after a good dose of the leaf tastes like so much chalk." And he corrects the duration downward: "the effect does not last for twenty-four hours as stated, but for only one or two hours." The DB should carry the one-to-two-hour figure, not the 24-hour one.

NO Shennong grade, no meridian entry: Gymnema sylvestre has no Bencao Gangmu entry. The stored tcm_pattern_match ('Damp-Heat in the Spleen/Stomach with Phlegm') is a modern cross-system inference with no pre-1900 Chinese warrant.

DATABASE INTEGRITY FLAG: the stored primary_text_citation quotes a Sushruta Samhita passage giving 'cooling in virya, with pungent vipaka' via Bhishagratna (1907-16). Post-1900 and unlocated. Given that Dymock says the plant is not even in the Raja Nighantu, a Sushruta attribution needs the Sanskrit original before it can stand.

results.pre1900_finding: COLD (sita), sweet (madhura), and — the addition the DB has no column for — HEAVY (guru guna). Dymock transmits the Nighantus directly: "heavy and cold, sweet, demulcent, galactogogue, tonic, and strengthening." The pre-1900 wording is 'cold', not 'cool'; the DB's 'Cool' is a mild softening of the classical reading, and its 'Moist' is supported by 'demulcent'.
results.evidence: Dymock, Warden & Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. III (Part VI), Bombay/London/Calcutta, 1893, p.483, s.v. ASPARAGUS RACEMOSUS, Willd. / ASPARAGUS SARMENTOSUS, Willd.: "These two plants appear to be the Satavari and Maha-satavari of the Nighantas: among the synonyms of the first, we find Dvipika, Dvipa-satru, Vara-ghantika, Narayani, and Sata-padi; the synonyms of the second are very similar, amongst them we note Bahu-puttrika, Dagdha, and Bhasma-roha. Both plants are considered to be heavy and cold, sweet, demulcent, galactogogue, tonic, and strengthening, and to remove bilious and rheumatic humors, blood diseases, and swellings; they are used both internally and in the preparation of several medicated oils." URL https://archive.org/download/pharmacographia03dymogoog/pharmacographia03dymogoog_djvu.txt (line 25650ff); volume title page reads PART VI ... 1893.
additions: GUNA CAPTURED EXPLICITLY: guru (HEAVY). This is the founder's ask realised — the DB has no guna column and 'heavy' is not decorative. Heavy substances are hard to digest, aggravate Kapha and are classically unsuitable where agni is weak. A cool-moist-sweet-heavy rasayana is a very different clinical object from a cool-moist-sweet one.

VIRYA: cold (sita), stated in those words. Note the pre-1900 reading is 'cold', while the DB stores 'Cool' — a one-step softening. Worth a founder decision on whether the DB tracks the source's own degree.
RASA: sweet (madhura) only, in the nighantu reading Dymock transmits. The DB stores 'Sweet, Bitter'. 'Bitter' has no pre-1900 support that I could reach.

VIPAKA: NOT STATED in any pre-1900 source I could reach. Dymock, Dutt 1877, Ainslie 1826 and Watt all omit post-digestive effect as a category. Leave the field empty rather than fill it — a plausible 'madhura vipaka' would be exactly the kind of invention the project has already been burned by.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE — and it is emphatic. The drug is chiefly a FAT-and-MILK medicine, not a powder. Dymock 1893: "The fresh juice of the root is given with honey as a demulcent in bilious dyspepsia or diarrhoea (Sarangadhara). As an aphrodisiac, Chakradatta directs four sers of the juice of the roots and four sers of ghi to be boiled in forty sers of milk, and to be flavoured with sugar or honey, and long pepper." And: "The chief use of the drug, however, is in the preparation of medicated oils for external application in nervous and rheumatic affections and urinary disorders" — the Narayana taila, whose full 20-plus-herb composition Dymock prints. A capsule of dried root powder is not the classical delivery form for any of the indications above.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the source's own idiom: galactogogue; tonic and strengthening; "to remove bilious and rheumatic humors, blood diseases, and swellings"; demulcent in bilious dyspepsia or diarrhoea; aphrodisiac in the ghee-and-milk preparation. The tubers are also "candied and eaten as a sweetmeat" — a food-grade, long-duration use.

SANSKRIT SYNONYMS recorded pre-1900: Satavari, Maha-satavari, Dvipika, Dvipa-satru, Vara-ghantika, Narayani, Sata-padi; for the greater kind, Bahu-puttrika, Dagdha, Bhasma-roha. Vernaculars: Satawar/Satavari (Hind., Guz., Mar.), Satamuli (Beng.), Kilavari (Tam.).

SPECIES DISCIPLINE — clean, but with one caveat the DB needs. Dymock treats A. racemosus TOGETHER WITH A. sarmentosus under one heading, so the 'heavy and cold, sweet' reading is transmitted for the pair, not for racemosus in isolation. Separately: this is NOT Asparagus cochinchinensis. The DB's tcm_pattern_match invites reading Shatavari 'through' Tian Men Dong 天門冬, which 本草從新 (1757) gives as 「甘苦大寒。入手太陰氣分（肺）…下通足少陰腎」 — sweet-bitter, GREATLY cold, entering Hand Taiyin (Lung) qi level and reaching down to Foot Shaoyin (Kidney). That is a different species with a colder assignment and a Lung-first channel entry; the cross-reading should be labelled as inference, not as Shatavari's own energetics.
NO Shennong grade: Asparagus racemosus has no Bencao Gangmu entry and therefore no 上/中/下 classification. The nearest Chinese grade belongs to 天門冬, a different species.

DATABASE INTEGRITY FLAG: the stored primary_text_citation names 'The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (Government of India, Ministry of AYUSH)' — an explicitly forbidden modern government standard — alongside an unlocated Charaka reference with a null URL and year 'classical'. The Dymock 1893 quotation above can replace it wholesale.

results.stored_temperature: Warm (prepared, Shu Di Huang); Cold (raw, Sheng Di Huang)
results.pre1900_finding: The classical texts give THREE states, not two, and the prepared form is 微温 SLIGHTLY warm, not warm. BCGM 1596: 生地黃 (fresh) 氣味大寒 GREATLY cold; 乾地黃 (dried) 氣味甘寒無毒 sweet and cold, with Zhen Quan dissenting 甘平 sweet-NEUTRAL; 熟地黃 (prepared) 氣味甘微苦微温無毒 sweet, slightly bitter, slightly warm. Crucially, Zhang Yuansu states the warmth is BORROWED FROM THE WINE, not intrinsic: 甘微苦寒，假酒力，酒蒸則微温而大補.
results.source_year: 1596 (Bencao Gangmu); corroborated 1799 recension of c. 200 CE text and 1757
results.evidence: 本草綱目 卷16 地黃 (李時珍, 1596). Dried: 「氣味甘寒無毒」…「别録曰苦，權曰甘平，好古曰甘苦寒，氣薄味厚，沈而降，隂也，入手足少隂厥隂及手太陽之經…日乾者平，火乾者温…元素曰生地黄大寒，胃弱者斟酌用之，恐損胃氣」. Fresh: 「生地黄氣味大寒」. Prepared: 「氣味甘微苦微温無毒」…「元素曰甘微苦寒，假酒力，酒蒸則微温而大補，味厚氣薄，隂中之陽，沈也，入手足少隂厥隂之經」. Li Shizhen's own summary rule: 「鮮用則寒，乾用則凉」. URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷16&action=raw — 神農本草經, 孫星衍輯本, 1799 (recension of c. 200 CE): 「干地黃 味甘，寒。主折跌絕筋，傷中，逐血痹，填骨髓，長肌肉，作湯，除寒熱積聚，除痹，生者尤良。久服，輕身、不老。一名地髓。生川澤。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw — 本草從新 (吳儀洛, 1757): 乾地黃「苦甘而寒，沉陰而降。入手足少陰（心、腎。）厥陰。（心包、肝。）及手太陽經。（小腸）」; 熟地黃「甘而微溫。入足三陰經。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 UPPER grade. BCGM heads the entry 「本經上品」 and Sun Xingyan's 1799 recension lists 干地黃 in the 草上品 index. The Bencao Jing text itself carries the long-use formula 「久服，輕身、不老」 — long use lightens the body and prevents ageing. This is an explicit classical warrant for sustained daily use, which is exactly the signal a daily-herb product needs and which the DB currently has no field to carry.

CHANNEL ENTRY (归经), stated three times over: 王好古 in BCGM 1596 — 「入手足少隂厥隂及手太陽之經」 (Hand and Foot Shaoyin = Heart and Kidney, Jueyin = Pericardium and Liver, plus Hand Taiyang = Small Intestine). 本草從新 1757 spells the organs out in-line: 乾地黃「入手足少陰（心、腎）厥陰（心包、肝）及手太陽經（小腸）」; 熟地黃「入足三陰經」 (the three foot yin channels: Spleen, Liver, Kidney). Note the shift — processing moves the drug from a four-channel Heart-inclusive profile to a three-foot-yin, Kidney-centred one.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE — the largest omission in the stored row. 九蒸九晒: BCGM 熟地黃修治 (Li Shizhen, 1596): 「以好酒入宿砂仁末在内拌勻，栁木甑於瓦鍋内蒸令氣透，㫰乾，再以砂仁酒拌蒸㫰，如此九蒸九㫰乃止」 — nine steamings and nine sun-dryings, in a willow-wood steamer over an earthen pot. HARD PROHIBITION, stated by 雷斆: 「勿犯銅鐵器，令人腎消并髮白，男損營，女損衛」 — it must never touch copper or iron vessels; doing so causes kidney-wasting and whitened hair, injuring ying in men and wei in women. DRYING METHOD CHANGES THE TEMPERATURE: 「日乾者平，火乾者温」 — sun-dried is neutral, fire-dried is warm. And the two correctives: 「薑汁浸則不泥膈，酒制則不妨」 — ginger-juice steeping stops it clogging the diaphragm, wine-processing stops it offending the stomach.

1757 DISSENT ON PREPARATION, worth storing because it contradicts the method the DB's own source-chain assumes. 吳儀洛, 本草從新: 「近時多拌以好酒及砂仁末而蒸晒之，是反以散动香燥、亂其性矣，其法甚爲不善」 — the fashionable wine-and-Amomum steaming disperses, aromatises and dries, disordering the herb's nature; the method is thoroughly bad. And on the market product: 「今市中惟以一煮而售，害有不可勝言者」 — what the shops sell is boiled ONCE, and the harm is beyond telling. Also: 「市醫尝將熟地枸杞等炒作炭用，是甘潤養陰之品，变而爲苦燥傷陰之物」 — charring it converts a sweet-moist yin-nourisher into a bitter-drying yin-damager.

CONTRAINDICATIONS AS STATED CLASSICALLY: BCGM 1596 — 「得清酒、麥門冬良；惡貝母；畏蕪荑」; 甄權: 「忌葱、蒜、蘿蔔、諸血，令人營衛澀，鬚髮白」 (avoid scallion, garlic, radish and blood-foods, which make ying and wei rough and whiten the hair); 張元素 on the fresh form: 「生地黄大寒，胃弱者斟酌用之，恐損胃氣」. 本草從新 1757, dried form: 「性寒而潤。脾虚泄瀉。胃虚食少。均在禁例」 — cold and moistening, so both spleen-deficiency diarrhoea and stomach-deficiency poor appetite are in the prohibited category. Prepared form: 「氣郁之人。能窒碍胸膈。用宜斟酌」 — in qi-constrained people it obstructs the chest and diaphragm. Virtually none of this is in the stored row, and the diarrhoea/poor-appetite exclusion is a real-world safety item.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the Bencao Jing's own idiom (1799 recension of the c. 200 CE text): 「主折跌絕筋，傷中，逐血痹，填骨髓，長肌肉，作湯除寒熱積聚，除痹，生者尤良。久服，輕身、不老。」 — fractures and severed sinews; internal damage; expels blood-impediment; FILLS THE MARROW; grows the flesh; decocted, dispels cold-heat accumulations and impediment; the fresh form is especially good. Note that the ancient indication set is orthopaedic and marrow-filling, which is upstream of the DB's yin-and-blood-tonic framing rather than identical to it.

FORMULA CONTEXT (no DB field): 王好古, in BCGM — 「仲景六味丸以之為諸藥之首，天一所生之源也；湯液四物湯治蔵血之臓，以之為君」. Chief of Liu Wei Di Huang Wan; sovereign in Si Wu Tang for the blood-storing viscus. Note the pairing with H092 in this same batch, where Dang Gui is sovereign and Di Huang the assistant — the role inverts by formula.

USE-DISCRIMINATION RULE the DB flattens: 王碩, quoted by Li Shizhen — 「男子多隂虚，宜用熟地黄；女子多血熱，宜用生地黄」. And 虞搏: 「生地黄生血而胃氣弱者服之恐妨食；熟地黄補血而痰飲多者服之恐泥膈」. The choice between raw and prepared is diagnostic, not merely a processing variant.
SPECIES: 地黃 = Rehmannia glutinosa throughout; 大明's floating test 「浮者名天黄，半浮半沈者名人黄，沈者名地黄，入藥沈者為佳」 is a grading rule for the same species, not a species distinction.

results.pre1900_finding: HOT and DRY, confirmed independently in both traditions and in the herb's own Sanskrit etymology. Indian: "Maricha is described in the Nighantas as bitter, pungent, digestive, hot and dry" (ushna virya, ruksha guna) — Dymock 1893. Chinese: BCGM 1596 head line 實氣味辛大温無毒 (pungent, greatly warm, non-toxic), with Li Shizhen's own gloss escalating it to 辛熱純陽 (pungent, HOT, pure yang); Wu Yiluo 1757 goes further still, 辛大熱。有毒 (pungent, greatly hot, TOXIC). The stored 'Hot' and 'Dry' are both correct; the stored 'Pungent' is correct but incomplete, the nighantus adding 'bitter'.
results.source_year: 1893 (Indian) and 1596 (Chinese)
results.evidence: Dymock, Warden & Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. III (Part VI), 1893, p.168: "Maricha is described in the Nighantas as bitter, pungent, digestive, hot and dry; synonyms for it are Valli-ja 'creeper grown,' Ushana, Tikshna 'pungent,' Malina, Syama 'black,' &c. It is said to be useful in intermittent fever, haemorrhoids, dyspepsia, cough, gonorrhoea and flatulence, and to promote the secretion of bile." Same page: "Black pepper is called in Sanskrit Maricha, which means a 'pungent berry.' The word is derived from Marichi, 'a particle of light or fire'." URL https://archive.org/download/pharmacographia03dymogoog/pharmacographia03dymogoog_djvu.txt (line 9515ff). — 本草綱目 卷32 胡椒 (李時珍, 1596): 「實氣味辛大温無毒」…「時珍曰辛熱純陽，走氣助火，昬目發瘡；珣曰多食損肺，令人吐血」. URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷32&action=raw — 本草從新 (吳儀洛, 1757): 「胡椒…辛大熱。有毒。溫中下氣。快膈消痰。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: THE ETYMOLOGY IS ITSELF A THERMAL CLAIM (Dymock 1893): Maricha derives from Marichi, "a particle of light or fire." And one of the classical synonyms IS the thermal word: Ushana. Other nighantu synonyms: Valli-ja ('creeper grown'), Tikshna ('pungent/sharp'), Malina, Syama ('black').

TRIKATU DOCTRINE, no DB field for it (Dymock 1893): "Together with long pepper and ginger it forms the much-used compound known as Trikatu, 'the three acrids,' or 'Ushana-chatu-rushana.'" Black pepper is classically a member of a triad, not a solo agent.
VIPAKA: NOT STATED in any pre-1900 source I could reach. Dymock gives rasa, virya and guna but no post-digestive effect. Leave empty.
GUNA captured: ruksha (DRY), stated in those words — "hot and dry." Confirms the DB's stored 'Dry'.

CHANNEL / SPHERE (Chinese): BCGM 1596 places it in the middle burner and the stomach-intestine axis — 「下氣温中去痰，除臟腑中風冷」; 「去胃口虚冷氣，宿食不消」; 「暖腸胃，除寒濕」. 本草從新 1757: 「溫中下氣。快膈消痰。」 No 归经 in formal channel terms is given by either text; the assignment is by burner and organ.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS, Indian (Dymock 1893): intermittent fever, haemorrhoids, dyspepsia, cough, gonorrhoea, flatulence; promotes the secretion of bile. Externally "a rubefacient and stimulant of the skin." Chinese (BCGM 1596): 「霍亂氣逆，心腹卒痛，冷氣上衝」; 「調五臟，壯腎氣，治冷痢，殺一切魚肉鼈蕈毒」; 「去胃寒吐水，大腸寒滑」; 「反胃虚脹，冷積隂毒，牙齒浮熱作痛」. Note the food-poisoning indication (fish, meat, turtle and mushroom toxins) — absent from the DB.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, Indian (Chakradatta via Dymock 1893), a seven-day protocol the DB has no room for: "A tablespoonful is boiled overnight in one seer of water, until the water is reduced to one-fourth of its bulk, the decoction is allowed to cool during the night, and is taken in the morning. The pepper is then again boiled in the same manner and the decoction taken at night. This treatment is continued for seven successive days."

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, Chinese (BCGM 1596) — an explicit toxicity-restraint pairing: 「近醫毎以緑豆同用治病有效，葢豆寒椒熱，隂陽配合得宜，且以豆制椒毒也」 — physicians pair it with mung bean, the bean being cold and the pepper hot, so that yin and yang are fittingly matched and the bean restrains the pepper's toxin.

CONTRAINDICATIONS, and they are the strongest in this batch. 李珣 (BCGM): 「多食損肺，令人吐血」 — eaten in quantity it injures the Lung and causes blood-vomiting. 朱震亨: 「胡椒屬火而性燥…積久則脾胃肺氣大傷，凡病氣疾人益大其禍也」. 李時珍: 「熱病人食之，䡃火傷氣，隂受其害」 and 「病咽喉口齒者亦宜忌之」 — also to be avoided in throat, mouth and tooth disease. Li Shizhen then gives a first-person case report, which is unusual and worth quoting to customers: 「時珍自少嗜之，嵗嵗病目而不疑及也；後漸知其害，遂痛絶之，目病亦止；纔食一二粒，即便昏澀」 — he loved it from boyhood, had eye disease every year without suspecting the cause, gave it up absolutely and the eye disease stopped; one or two grains would bring the blurring straight back. 吳儀洛 1757: 「損肺走氣。动火动血。損齒昏目。發瘡痔臟毒。必陰氣至足者，方可用」 — only a person whose yin is fully sufficient may use it at all.

NO SHENNONG GRADE, and this matters. 胡椒 enters the Chinese record at the 唐本草 (Tang Xinxiu Bencao, 659 CE), not the Bencao Jing, so it carries no 上/中/下 classification; BCGM notes 「校正：自木部移入此」. A substance with no upper-grade warrant, an explicit 1757 有毒 toxicity note, and a named author's account of self-injury from habitual use is not a daily-tonic candidate — it is a corrective for cold, used short.

SPECIES: Piper nigrum confirmed on both sides. BCGM records the Sanskrit-derived name and the Indian origin: 「胡椒出摩伽陁國，呼為昧履支」 (from Magadha, called marica) — the same word Dymock gives as Maricha. This is a rare case of the two traditions demonstrably naming the same drug.

NOTE ON THE STORED CITATION: the DB's primary cites King's American Dispensatory (Felter & Lloyd, 1898), which IS pre-1900 and therefore admissible by date, though I did not verify its content in this pass. The stored SECONDARY cites Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931) and AHPA 2013 — both inadmissible.

results.pre1900_finding: The head-reading in BOTH the Han-dynasty text and the Bencao Gangmu is 平 NEUTRAL, not cool. Shennong Bencao Jing: 味苦，平 (bitter, neutral). BCGM 1596: 氣味苦平無毒. 'Cool/cold' is the 名醫別錄 minority reading — 別録曰㣲寒 (slightly cold) — which Wu Yiluo carries forward in 1757 as 苦微寒. Two pre-1900 readings, sharply divergent, and per the project's own rule they should both be stored rather than adjudicated. The stored 'Cool' silently picks the minority line.
results.source_year: 1799 (Sun Xingyan recension of the c. 200 CE Bencao Jing) and 1596 (Bencao Gangmu)
results.evidence: 神農本草經, 孫星衍・孫馮翼輯本, 1799 (recension of the c. 200 CE original): 「柴胡 味苦，平。主心腹，去腸胃中結氣，飲食積聚，寒熱邪氣，推陳致新。久服，輕身、明目、益精。一名地熏。《吳普》曰：茈葫，一名山菜，一名茹草，神農、岐伯、雷公：苦，無毒，生冤句。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=神農本草經_(孫星衍)&action=raw — 本草綱目 卷13 茈胡 (李時珍, 1596), headed 「本經上品」: 「氣味苦平無毒」…「别録曰㣲寒，普曰神農岐伯雷公苦無毒，大明曰甘，元素曰氣味俱輕，陽也，升也，少陽經藥，引胃氣上升，苦寒以發散表熱；杲曰升也，隂中之陽，手足少陽厥隂四經引經藥也」. URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷13&action=raw — 本草從新 (吳儀洛, 1757): 「柴胡…苦微寒。味薄氣升爲陽。主陽氣下陷。能引清氣上行。而平少陽厥陰之邪熱。」 URL https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=本草從新&action=raw
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 上品 UPPER grade. BCGM heads the entry 「本經上品」 and Sun Xingyan's 1799 recension lists 柴胡 in the 草上品 index. The Bencao Jing text carries the long-use formula 「久服，輕身、明目、益精」 — long use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, augments essence. Together with H104 this is one of only two upper-grade herbs in the batch, and the grade is precisely the duration signal a daily-herb product needs.

CHANNEL ENTRY (归经), the richest in this batch. 張元素 (BCGM 1596): 「少陽經藥，引胃氣上升」. 李杲: 「手足少陽厥隂四經引經藥也」 — a CHANNEL-GUIDING herb for four channels, Hand and Foot Shaoyang and Hand and Foot Jueyin. 李時珍's pairing rule: 「行手足少陽以黄芩為佐，行手足厥隂以黄連為佐」 — to drive it into Shaoyang, assist with Huang Qin; into Jueyin, assist with Huang Lian. 本草從新 1757: 「爲足少陽胆經表藥」 — the exterior-resolving herb of the Foot Shaoyang Gallbladder channel.

DEPTH/DIRECTION RULE (王好古, BCGM 1596): 「在經主氣，在臓主血」 — in the channels it governs qi, in the viscera it governs blood. And the part-and-processing rule: 「欲上升則用根，以酒浸；欲中及下降則用稍」 — to make it ascend use the ROOT steeped in wine; for the middle burner and for descending use the ROOTLET/TIP. 本草從新 1757 repeats: 「凡治中及下降用梢。」 The DB stores one undifferentiated 'Root'.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE — a hard prohibition (BCGM 卷13 根脩治, 雷斆, 1596): 「凡采得銀州柴胡，去鬚及頭，用銀刀削去赤薄皮少許，以粗布拭淨剉用，勿令犯火，立便無效也」 — remove the beard and head, pare off a little of the thin red skin WITH A SILVER KNIFE, wipe clean with coarse cloth, cut for use, and DO NOT LET IT MEET FIRE, or it is instantly without effect. 本草從新 1757 gives the indication-specific refinement: 「外感生用。内傷升氣酒炒用…有汗咳者。蜜水拌炒。」 — raw for external contraction; wine-fried to raise qi in internal damage; honey-water-fried where there is cough with sweating.

CONTRAINDICATIONS AS STATED CLASSICALLY: 之才 (BCGM 1596): 「半夏為之使，惡皂莢，畏女菀、藜蘆」. 本草從新 1757: 「陰虚火炎氣升者。禁用。」 — forbidden where yin is deficient with fire flaring and qi rising. And the strongest classical safety statement in this batch, 寇宗奭 printed in the BCGM: 「柴胡本經並無一字治勞，今人治勞方中鮮有不用者，嗚呼，凡此誤世甚多…若此等病茍無實熱，醫者執而用之，不死何待」 — the Bencao Jing says not one word about Chai Hu treating taxation; if there is no REAL heat and a physician insists on using it, death need not wait long. Li Shizhen answers him but does not dismiss the rule: 「惟勞在肺腎者不用可爾」.

ADULTERATION AND SOURCING CAUTION, stated in the sources themselves — directly relevant to a commercial product. BCGM 1596: 「近時有一種根似桔梗沙參，白色而大，市人以偽充銀柴胡，殊無氣味，不可不辨」. 本草從新 1757 is blunter: 「今藥客入山收买，將白頭翁、丹參、小前胡、遠志苗等俱雜在内，謂之統柴胡。藥肆中俱切爲飲片。其實真柴胡無幾。」 — the traders mix in Bai Tou Weng, Dan Shen, small Qian Hu and Yuan Zhi shoots, sell it as 'general chai hu', slice it into decoction pieces, and very little of it is real Chai Hu. Wu Yiluo also lists 銀州柴胡 as a SEPARATE sub-entry for 虚劳肌熱、骨蒸劳瘧 — a distinct drug (Stellaria dichotoma in later usage) that must not be conflated with Bupleurum.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the Bencao Jing's own idiom (1799 recension of c. 200 CE): 「主心腹，去腸胃中結氣，飲食積聚，寒熱邪氣，推陳致新」 — governs the heart and abdomen, removes bound qi in the stomach and intestines, food accumulations, cold-heat evil qi, and PUSHES OUT THE OLD TO BRING ON THE NEW (推陳致新). The Bielu layer adds 「除傷寒心下煩熱，諸痰熱結實，胸中邪逆，五臟間遊氣，大腸停積水脹，及濕痺拘攣，亦可作浴湯」 — and note the last clause: it may also be made into a bathing decoction, an external route the DB does not record.

NOMENCLATURE FACT: the Bencao Gangmu heads the entry 茈胡, not 柴胡, and Li Shizhen explains the reading: 「茈字有柴紫二音…茈胡之茈音柴。茈胡生山中，嫩則可茹，老則采而為柴，故苖有芸蒿、山菜、茹草之名，而根名柴胡也」. Anyone grepping these texts for 柴胡 will miss the BCGM head-entry entirely.

SPECIES: Bupleurum, confirmed by the 集解 descriptions (銀州/北柴胡 preferred; 南土所産者…强硬不堪使用). The classical texts do not distinguish B. chinense from B. scorzonerifolium; they distinguish by PROVENANCE (Yinzhou/northern good, southern unusable), which is a different axis from the DB's single latin_name.

results.pre1900_finding: BCGM 1596 assigns 氣味苦濇微溫無毒 — bitter, astringent, SLIGHTLY warm (微溫), non-toxic — to the root as such. The classical text makes NO raw-vs-prepared thermal distinction: Li Shizhen describes the nine-steam/nine-sun black-soybean processing in detail yet still gives one single 微溫 reading for the drug. The DB's 'neutral to cool (raw)' has no pre-1900 warrant in this source. He Shou Wu is absent from the Shennong Bencao Jing entirely (BCGM marks it 宋開寶, i.e. entering the canon with the Kaibao Bencao, 973 CE), so it carries NO Shennong grade.
results.evidence: 氣味 line, verbatim: 「氣味苦濇微溫無毒」. Li Shizhen's 發明, verbatim: 「時珍曰何首烏足厥隂少隂藥也白者入氣分赤者入血分…此物氣溫味苦濇苦補腎温補肝能收斂精氣所以能養血益肝固精益腎健筋骨烏髭髪為滋補良藥不寒不燥功在地黃天門冬諸藥之上」. The 集解 quotes Li Ao's 何首烏傳 (813 CE): 「何首烏味甘性溫無毒茯苓為使」. — Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目 (Bencao Gangmu), 卷十八上 草之七 蔓草類, entry 何首烏, YEAR 1596 (Siku Quanshu recension, traditional characters). URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E7%B6%B1%E7%9B%AE_(%E5%9B%9B%E5%BA%AB%E5%85%A8%E6%9B%B8%E6%9C%AC)/%E5%8D%B718%E4%B8%8A (raw text via ?action=raw). Read directly in the original Chinese; no modern translation used.
additions: CHANNEL ENTRY (归经), stated outright and the DB has no column for it: 「何首烏足厥隂少隂藥也」 — a foot-Jueyin (Liver) and foot-Shaoyin (Kidney) medicine. Li Shizhen adds a colour split the DB also lacks: 「白者入氣分赤者入血分」 — the WHITE root enters the qi aspect, the RED root the blood aspect. Red and white He Shou Wu are two different clinical drugs in 1596, and the classical tonic formulas use them TOGETHER in equal weight (赤白何首烏各一斤).

SHENNONG GRADE: none. He Shou Wu is not in the Shennong Bencao Jing; BCGM tags it 宋開寶 (Kaibao Bencao, 973 CE). For a product that uses Shennong grade to encode duration-of-use, this herb simply has no such warrant, and the 'daily, indefinitely' framing rests on the Li Ao legend (fasting immortality tale) rather than on a graded classical authority.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, mandatory and specific in 1596: 「用何首烏赤白各一斤竹刀刮去粗皮米泔浸一夜切片用黒豆三斗毎次用三升三合三勺以水泡過砂鍋内鋪豆一層首烏一層重重鋪盡蒸之豆熟取出去豆將何首烏晒乾再以豆蒸如此九蒸九晒乃用」 — nine steamings and nine sun-dryings over black soybeans, cut with a BAMBOO knife (竹刀 / 苦竹刀), soaked overnight in rice-washing water. Lei Xiao's older method adds 忌鐵器 — iron implements forbidden.

CONTRAINDICATIONS / INCOMPATIBILITIES as stated classically: 「茯苓為之使忌諸血無鱗魚蘿蔔蒜葱鐵器同于地黄能伏硃砂」 — Poria is its envoy; avoid all blood, scaleless fish, radish, garlic, onion and iron vessels. The 何首烏傳 adds a dosing rite: 「凡服用偶日二四六八日服訖以衣覆汗出導引尤良忌猪肉血羊血無鱗魚觸藥無力」 — take on even-numbered days; pork blood, mutton blood and scaleless fish neutralise the drug.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the source's idiom: 「主治瘰癧消癰腫療頭面風瘡治五痔止心痛益血氣黑髭髮悦顔色久服長筋骨益精髓延年不老亦治婦人産後及帶下諸疾」 (開寶); 「瀉肝風」 (王好古). Note that the FIRST-listed classical indication is 瘰癧 (scrofula / neck lumps) and 癰腫 — sores and swellings — not hair-blackening; the cosmetic reputation is a Ming-dynasty vogue Li Shizhen dates precisely to the Jiajing era (嘉靖初) after 七寶美髯丹 was presented to the emperor.

THERMAL NUANCE the DB flattens: Li Shizhen explicitly positions it as neither cold nor drying — 「為滋補良藥不寒不燥功在地黃天門冬諸藥之上」 — i.e. its virtue is that it tonifies WITHOUT the coldness of Rehmannia/Asparagus. That is an argument about temperature, and it is the reason the classical tradition prefers it, worth surfacing on a monograph.

NOT FOUND pre-1900: any statement of hepatotoxicity. The 1596 text says 無毒 (non-toxic). The liver-injury signal in the DB's secondary citation is entirely modern and must not be attributed to the classical record.

results.pre1900_finding: NO pre-1900 source assigns Sariva an explicit virya. I checked five: Ainslie, Materia Indica (1826); U. C. Dutt, Materia Medica of the Hindus (1877); Dymock, Vegetable Materia Medica of Western India (1885); Dymock/Warden/Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica (1891); Watt, Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (1890). Every one of them gives TASTE (sweet/madhura) and ACTIONS (demulcent, alterative, tonic) and stops there. None states sita, none states 'cooling' of the drug itself. The closest any comes is Dymock's report of a LOCAL SENSATION and a heat INDICATION, neither of which is a virya assignment. Per the project rule that an action word is not a temperature, the stored 'Cool' is unsupported by any source published 1899 or earlier that I could reach.
results.evidence: Dutt, verbatim: "The roots of these plants are said to be sweet, demulcent, alterative and useful in loss of appetite, disinclination for food, fever, skin diseases, syphilis and leucorrhoea." — Udoy Chand Dutt, The Materia Medica of the Hindus, Compiled from Sanskrit Medical Works, Calcutta, pp. 195-196, YEAR 1877. URL: https://archive.org/details/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft (OCR: https://archive.org/download/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft_djvu.txt). Dymock, verbatim: "The Hindus consider them to be demulcent, alterative and tonic, and prescribe them in dyspepsia, skin diseases, syphilis, fever and dysentery" — Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. II, p. 446, YEAR 1891, https://archive.org/details/b21960343_0002. Watt, verbatim: "the Hindus consider both as tonic, sweet, demulcent, and alterative" — Dictionary of the Economic Products of India, Vol. IV, p. 230, YEAR 1890, https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.83717. The only near-thermal statement anywhere, Dymock 1885, verbatim: "the milky juice is dropped into inflamed eyes; it causes copious lacrymation, and afterwards a sensation of coolness in the part" and the root "administered with ghi as a remedy in heat or inflammation of the urinary passages" — The Vegetable Materia Medica of Western India, 2nd ed., pp. 510-511, YEAR 1885, https://archive.org/details/b20416349. A sensation and an indication; not a virya.
additions: THE SPECIES PROBLEM IS THE HEADLINE HERE, and it is pre-1900 documented. Dutt 1877, verbatim: "In Sanskrit Medicine, Hemidesmus Indicus and Ichnocarpus frutescens are both called sdrivd and are described under the name of sdrivddvaya or the two sdrivds… When however sdrivd is used in the singular number it is the usual practice to interpret it as sydmalatd (Ichnocarpus frutescens)." So the classical Sanskrit head-word SARIVA, used alone, points to ICHNOCARPUS, not Hemidesmus. A monograph on Hemidesmus indicus that inherits classical 'Sariva' attributes is taking properties the 1877 authority assigns to a different plant. Dymock 1885 and Watt 1890 both repeat this. Hemidesmus is distinguished as उत्पलसारिवा Utpala-sariva.

SANSKRIT SYNONYMS the DB lacks, from Dymock 1891 and Watt 1890: Anantamula (अनन्तमूल, 'endless root'), Nagajihva ('snake's tongue'), Gopa-kanya ('cowherd's daughter'), Sugandhi, Gopi-mulam. Arabic/Persian: Zaiyan, Aushbatunnar, Aushbah-e-Hindi. Tamil Nannari.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, from Dymock 1885/1891 (Konkan practice), verbatim: "The root is tied up in plantain leaves and roasted in hot ashes; it is then beaten into a mass with cumin and sugar and administered with ghi as a remedy in heat or inflammation of the urinary passages." Ash-roasting in plantain leaf, then a ghee vehicle — a real vehicle doctrine the DB has no field for. Dutt 1877 gives the classical pairing instead: anantamula with bala (Pavonia odorata), mustaka (Cyperus rotundus), ginger and katuki (Picrorrhiza kurroa), equal parts, as a paste taken with warm water in the morning.

POTENCY / STORAGE DOCTRINE, Watt 1890, verbatim: "There seems to be no doubt that the roots ought to be employed when fairly fresh, and that their medicinal virtues decrease greatly as they become old and dried up." Watt also warns the commercial root "is often so old as to be quite worthless." Directly relevant to a product sourcing this herb.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the sources' own idiom: loss of appetite and 'disinclination for food' (aruchi), fever, skin diseases, syphilis, leucorrhoea, dyspepsia, dysentery, gravel and strangury; and per Ainslie 1826, verbatim, the Tamil physicians give it "in decoction, in conjunction with cummin seeds, to purify the blood, and correct the acrimony of the bile" (Materia Indica, Vol. I, p. 382). 'Correcting the acrimony of the bile' is the nearest thing to a pitta rationale anywhere in the pre-1900 record.

VIPAKA and GUNA: not stated in any pre-1900 source reached. Do not fill these in. The Bhavaprakasha Nighantu vargas are not carried on Sanskrit Wikisource (only the Samhita's chikitsa sections are), and I would not cite a modern printed Nighantu edition as the original.

results.pre1900_finding: Confirmed, but by the UNANI route, not the Ayurvedic one. The Muhammadan (Yunani) writers, reported by Dymock from the Makhzan-el-Adwiya, class bdellium/mukul as HOT AND DRY — an explicit Galenic thermal-plus-moisture assignment, which also independently confirms the stored moisture value 'Dry'. On the Ayurvedic side the pre-1900 record is silent on virya: Dutt 1877 and Dymock 1885/1890 both give only actions ('demulcent, aperient, alterative, and a purifier of the blood'). So 'Warm' stands on a pre-1900 source, but the DB should record that the warrant is Unani.
results.evidence: Verbatim: "Good Bdellium should be clean, bright, sticky, soft, sweet-smelling, yellowish, and bitter; when burnt it smells like Bay; it mixes readily with water, and is described as hot and dry; from the account of its properties in the Makhzan-el-Adwiya, it would appear to be used in very nearly the same way as myrrh." — William Dymock, C. J. H. Warden and David Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica: A History of the Principal Drugs of Vegetable Origin met with in British India, Vol. I, Burseraceae, p. 312, YEAR 1890. URL: https://archive.org/details/b21960343_0001 (OCR: https://archive.org/download/b21960343_0001/b21960343_0001_djvu.txt). Corroborating the DRY reading only, and giving the Ayurvedic side without a virya, Dutt verbatim: "Guggulu [ is ] said to be demulcent, aperient, alterative and a purifier of the blood." — U. C. Dutt, The Materia Medica of the Hindus, pp. 132-133, YEAR 1877, https://archive.org/details/materiamedicaofh00duttuoft.
additions: SPECIES / SOURCE-PLANT WARNING, pre-1900 and explicit. Dymock argues the Sanskrit GUGGULU is probably NOT a Commiphora at all. Verbatim, 1890: "Sanskrit writers describe Guggulu as moist, viscid, fragrant, and of a golden colour when freshly exuded — a description which is not applicable to the exudation of the Balsamodendrons, but is exactly so to the exudation of B. serrata." i.e. he reads classical guggulu as BOSWELLIA SERRATA, and says the Balsamodendron product is distinguished in the Bombay bazaar as Mhaisa-gugal ('buffalo guggul'). Dutt 1877 by contrast heads his entry BALSAMODENDRON MUKUL. Two pre-1900 authorities, two different plants, and the DB currently records only one. Do not adjudicate this; surface it.

GRADE / CLASS in the Sanskrit system, and it is the DURATION-relevant fact: guggulu is named a RASAYANA in the Bhavaprakasha's own definition verse, verbatim Sanskrit: 「रसायनन्तु तज्ज्ञेयं यज्जराव्याधिनाशनम् । यथा हरीतकी दन्ती गुग्गुलुश्च शिलाजतु ॥२२९॥」 — 'that is to be known as rasayana which destroys ageing and disease, as haritaki, danti, guggulu and shilajatu.' Bhavamishra, Bhavaprakasha Samhita, Purvakhanda, 16th century; Sanskrit text at https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B6%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%82%E0%A4%B9%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE/%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%82%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%96%E0%A4%A3%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A1%E0%A4%83 (quoted in the original Devanagari, not from a translation).

PREPARATION DOCTRINE — freshness is a hard classical rule, and it is a purchasing spec. Dutt 1877, verbatim: "According to Sanskrit writers, new or recently exuded guggulu is moist, viscid, fragrant and of a golden colour. It burns in the fire, melts in the sun and forms a milky emulsion with hot water. Old guggulu is dry and without flavour or colour; IT SHOULD NOT BE USED IN MEDICINE." The DB's part_used says 'purified oleo-gum-resin (shodhita guggulu)' but carries no freshness criterion; 1877 gives four testable ones (burns, melts in sun, emulsifies in hot water, golden).

VEHICLE DOCTRINE the DB lacks: guggulu is never given bare. Dutt 1877's Yogaraja guggulu is rubbed together with GHEE and stored in an earthen pot itself smeared with ghee; Dymock 1890's Bombay version is taken with a decoction of Sphaeranthus indicus. Aditya-paka guggulu soaks its aromatics seven days in dasamula decoction BEFORE the resin is added.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the sources' idiom: rheumatism, 'diseases supposed to be caused by deranged air' (vata) — Dutt's rendering of vata-vyadhi — unhealthy ulcerations, affections of the joints, rheumatism of the loins and sacrum (Trayodasanga guggulu), nervous diseases and paralysis, scrofulous affections, urinary disorders, skin diseases. Dymock 1890 adds the Unani/Bombay practice: "Indian Bdellium combined with Black pepper and Colchicum has a reputation in muscular rheumatism; it is given internally, and also applied to the painful part as a lip [lep, a paste]." External paste use is absent from the DB.

VIPAKA and GUNA: not stated in any pre-1900 source reached. The DB's 'Bitter, Pungent, Astringent' taste and 'lekhana/medohara' framing are not verbatim in Dutt 1877 or Dymock; the pre-1900 English record calls it demulcent and aperient, which sits oddly with 'scraping'. Flag for founder review rather than treating the modern lekhana reading as classical.

results.pre1900_finding: Three independent pre-1900 Chinese sources give 平 NEUTRAL, not cool. Shennong Bencao Jing: 味甘，平. BCGM 1596: 葛根氣味甘辛平無毒 (sweet, acrid, neutral, non-toxic). Ben Cao Cong Xin 1757: 辛甘性平. The ONLY cold reading in the classical record is attached to a different preparation — the FRESH ROOT JUICE, which the Mingyi Bielu calls 大寒 (greatly cold). The DB's part_used is the dried root, so it has inherited the fresh-juice temperature. Wang Haogu is quoted in BCGM saying so flatly: 氣平味甘.
results.evidence: BCGM verbatim: 「葛根氣味甘辛平無毒」 with the attached note 「别錄曰生根汁大寒好古曰氣平味甘升也陽也陽明經行經的藥也」 — Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目, 卷十八上 草之七 蔓草類, entry 葛, marked 本經中品, YEAR 1596. URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E7%B6%B1%E7%9B%AE_(%E5%9B%9B%E5%BA%AB%E5%85%A8%E6%9B%B8%E6%9C%AC)/%E5%8D%B718%E4%B8%8A. Shennong Bencao Jing verbatim: 「葛根 味甘，平。主消渴，身大熱，嘔吐，諸痺，起陰氣，解諸毒，葛谷，主下利十歲以上。一名雞齊根。」 — 神農本草經, 孫星衍 Sun Xingyan & Sun Fengyi recension, YEAR 1799, https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E7%A5%9E%E8%BE%B2%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E7%B6%93_(%E5%AD%AB%E6%98%9F%E8%A1%8D). Ben Cao Cong Xin verbatim: 「辛甘性平。輕扬升發。入陽明經。能鼓胃氣上行。生津止渴。」 and separately 「生葛汁大寒。解溫病大熱。」 — 吳儀洛 Wu Yiluo, 本草從新, YEAR 1757, https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E5%BE%9E%E6%96%B0. All read in the original Chinese.
additions: SHENNONG GRADE: 中品, MIDDLE grade. BCGM tags the entry 「葛 本經中品」 and the Sun Xingyan 1799 recension places 葛根 in 卷二·中經 under 上草，中品四十九種. The Shennong preface defines the middle grade as 「中藥一百二十種為臣，主養性以應人。無毒、有毒，斟酌其宜。欲遏病補羸者，本中經」 — ministers, some toxic some not, to be weighed for suitability, for checking disease. This is NOT an upper-grade 'take daily forever' herb by the classical scheme, and a product recommending daily herbs should reflect that.

CHANNEL ENTRY (归经), stated in two independent pre-1900 sources: 王好古 in BCGM — 「陽明經行經的藥也」, a Yangming channel-conducting medicine; Li Shizhen's 發明 — 「葛根乃陽明經藥兼入脾經脾主肌肉」, Yangming channel medicine also entering the Spleen, and the spleen governs the flesh (which is the classical rationale for its action on the muscle layer, and the DB states the effect without the reason). Wu Yiluo 1757 repeats: 「入陽明經…兼入脾經」.

PART / PREPARATION DOCTRINE the DB does not capture: FRESH root juice (生葛汁), DRIED root (乾葛), and the starch (葛粉) are three different medicines with different temperatures and uses. 生葛汁 is 大寒 and is the form used for 心熱吐血, 衂血不止, 熱毒下血 and 酒醉不醒. Li Gao on the dried form, verbatim: 「乾葛其氣輕浮鼓舞胃氣上行生津液又解肌熱治脾胃虛弱泄瀉聖藥也」. The seed 葛穀 (甘平) and the flower 葛花 are separate drugs — 葛花 for 消酒, hangover.

CONTRAINDICATIONS as stated classically, three of them, none in the DB: (1) 張元素 — 「升陽生津脾虚作渴者非此不除勿多用恐傷胃氣」, do not use much, it may injure stomach qi; (2) 朱震亨 — 「凡㿀痘已見紅㸃不可用葛根升麻湯恐表虚反増㿀爛也」, once pox spots have appeared do not give Ge Gen decoctions, they weaken the exterior and worsen ulceration; (3) 陳藏器 — 「生者墮胎」, the raw root causes miscarriage. Wu Yiluo 1757 adds a constitutional exclusion: 「上盛下虚之人。虽有脾胃病。亦不宜服…夏月表虚汗多、尤忌。」 — those full above and deficient below should not take it even for a spleen-stomach complaint, and it is especially forbidden in summer with exterior deficiency and profuse sweating.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the source's own idiom (本經): 「主消渴，身大熱，嘔吐，諸痺，起陰氣，解諸毒」 — wasting-thirst, great body heat, vomiting, the bi obstructions, RAISING THE YIN QI, resolving the poisons. 別錄 adds 「療傷寒中風頭痛解肌發表出汗開腠理療金瘡止脇風痛」. 之才 adds a specific antidotal claim the DB lacks: 「殺野葛巴豆百藥毒」 — it kills the poison of Gelsemium, croton and a hundred drugs.

DISSENT WORTH PRINTING: this herb's temperature is contested only across PREPARATIONS, not across authorities. Every pre-1900 source I read agrees the root is 平 and the fresh juice is 大寒. That is a cleaner, more defensible story than 'Cool', and it changes the product recommendation (a dried-root tea is not a cooling herb by the classical record).

results.herb: Red Sage / Dan Shen — Salvia miltiorrhiza
results.pre1900_finding: The head-reading matches exactly. Shennong Bencao Jing: 丹參 味苦，微寒 — bitter, SLIGHTLY COLD. BCGM 1596 carries the same: 根氣味苦微寒無毒. But the classical record around that line is unusually contested and the DB should not present 'cool' as settled: Li Dangzhi read 大寒 (greatly cold), Zhen Quan read 平 (neutral), Tao Hongjing argued the drug is actually HOT and that 微寒 is an error, and Li Shizhen's OWN 發明 says 氣平. Wu Yiluo 1757 likewise opens 氣平而降.
results.evidence: BCGM verbatim: 「根氣味苦微寒無毒」 with the attached note 「普曰神農桐君黄帝雷公苦無毒岐伯鹹李當之大寒𢎞景曰乆服多眼赤故應性熱今云微寒恐謬也權曰平之才曰畏鹽水反藜蘆」 — Tao Hongjing: 'long use causes red eyes, so its nature ought to be HOT; the present reading 微寒 is I fear an error.' Li Shizhen's own 發明, verbatim: 「丹參色赤味苦氣平而降隂中之陽也入手少隂厥隂之經心與包絡血分藥也」. — 李時珍, 本草綱目, 卷十二下 草之一 山草類下, entry 丹參, marked 本經上品, YEAR 1596.
