additions: VIPAKA, stated explicitly and matching the stored taste field: कटुका पाके — PUNGENT (katu) in vipaka, with tikta as the rasa (BPN 2.152). This is one of the few rows where the database already carries vipaka; the pre-1900 source confirms it verbatim.

GUNA: रूक्षा (ruksha, DRY) and लघुः (laghu, LIGHT). Both nighantus and Dymock 1893 agree — Dymock's English "dry… light" is a direct rendering of ruksha and laghu. The stored moisture 'Dry' is therefore classically supported, unlike several other rows in this batch. LAGHU is new information the database has no column for and it matters: a light, dry, cold bitter behaves differently from a heavy cold one.

CHINESE READING IS SPLIT AND SHOULD BE REPORTED, NOT RESOLVED: the BCGM 1596 head line gives 苦平 (bitter, NEUTRAL) while the attached note gives 「㳟曰大寒」 — Su Gong: VERY COLD. So within one 1596 entry the Chinese record carries both 'neutral' and 'very cold' for this drug. The Sanskrit sources are unanimous for cold; the Chinese record is not.
CHANNEL ENTRY (归经): not given for 胡黃連 in the BCGM entry. The stated organ targets are functional — 補肝膽明目 (supplements Liver and Gallbladder, brightens the eyes).

CONTRAINDICATIONS, classical and severe: (1) BCGM 1596 — 「惡菊花𤣥參白鮮皮解巴豆毒忌猪肉令人漏精」: it hates chrysanthemum, xuanshen and baixianpi; it antidotes badou poison; AVOID PORK, which causes seminal leakage. (2) Wu Yiluo, 本草從新, 1757, 胡黃連, quoting Yu Jiayan: 「膽草、蘆薈、黃連、胡黃連之類、極苦大寒、兒不能勝爾…胃虚者服之、有死而已」 — extremely bitter and very cold; children cannot withstand it, and those with a deficient stomach who take it simply die. That is as blunt a classical contraindication as this project will find, and it is aimed precisely at the paediatric use the herb is famous for. (URL https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E5%BE%9E%E6%96%B0 ; this transcription is mixed simplified, so treat as locate-only, not quotable as the 1757 text.)

PREPARATION DOCTRINE: Dymock 1893 records the standard vehicle — "given daily in decoction, with liquorice, raisins, and Neem bark, half a tola (90 grains) of each, water 32 tolas, boiled down to one-fourth", and "Chakradatta states that about two drachms of the powdered root given with sugar and warm water act as a gentle aperient." The sweet co-drugs (liquorice, raisins, sugar) are doctrine, not garnish: they buffer an intensely bitter cold drug. U. C. Dutt, 1877, p. 186, records it inside Susruta's Shaddharana yoga with plumbago root, indrayava, patha, atis and chebulic myrobalan.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the sources' own idiom: BPN 2.152 — भेदिनी (purgative), दीपनी (kindles digestion), हृद्या; removes कफ, पित्त, ज्वर; destroys प्रमेह, श्वास, कास, अस्र (blood disorders), दाह (burning), कुष्ठ, कृमि. RN 5.132 — conquers पित्त and अस्र-दोष; removes बलास (kapha), अरोचक (anorexia), श्वास, ज्वर. BCGM 1596 — 骨蒸勞熱 (steaming-bone taxation heat), 三消, 五心煩熱, 婦人胎蒸, 虚驚, 冷熱洩痢, 五痔, 久痢成疳, 小兒驚癎, 溫瘧, 去果子積.

SPECIES: correctly pinned. Dymock's 1893 heading is PICRORHIZA KURROOA, Benth., and he confirms the identification from a specimen supplied by J. F. Duthie from Kumaon. He also documents the historic trap: "Mahometan writers give Katki or Kutki as an Indian synonym for black Hellebore, and unmistakably describe the latter plant… This mistake has misled most European writers upon Indian drugs." Separately, the Chinese 胡黃連 is described in BCGM as 「出波斯國」 (from Persia), i.e. an imported drug — so the Chinese entry is evidence about an Indian/Central Asian import and cannot be assumed to be Picrorhiza scrophulariiflora.

results.herb: Maitake (Hen of the Woods) — Grifola frondosa

Full-text searches of Chinese and Japanese Wikisource for 灰樹花, 栗蘑, 千佛菌 and 舞茸 return no materia medica hit.

additions: THE STORED CITATION IS NOT SUPPORTABLE AND SHOULD BE PULLED. The row's primary_text_citation asserts that Li Shizhen's Bencao Gangmu (1596) treats maitake as "hui shu hua, 'grey tree flower'", a spleen and stomach tonic. I checked the 1596 fungus section in the Siku Quanshu recension directly. There is no such entry, and 灰樹花 does not occur anywhere in it. The name 灰樹花 is a modern Chinese mycological coinage. This is a fabricated attribution of exactly the kind this project has already been burned by, and it is currently sitting in the production row.

THE ROW'S tcm_pattern_match IS ALSO UNSOURCED. Statements that maitake "enters the Spleen, Stomach, and Lung", "builds defensive Qi", and was "traditionally said to… settle the hemorrhoids, and calm the spirit" have no pre-1900 warrant that I could find. Note that 「治痔」 (treats haemorrhoids) IS the classical claim for 雞㙡 (BCGM 1596: 「氣味甘平無毒主治益胃清神治痔」) — a different mushroom entirely. The maitake text reads like 雞㙡's attributes transplanted.

WHAT COULD LEGITIMATELY BE SAID INSTEAD: if the founder wants a classical framing for maitake, the honest one is by analogy and must be labelled as such — the BCGM's food-tonic fungi as a class run 甘平 (sweet, neutral): 香蕈 甘平無毒, 天花蕈 甘平無毒, 雞㙡 甘平無毒, with 蘑菰蕈 the outlier at 甘寒無毒. So 'Neutral' is a defensible class inference. It is not a sourced attribution, and must not be dressed as one.
NO SHENNONG GRADE — the herb is absent from the Shennong Bencao Jing entirely, as it is from every pre-1900 bencao I could reach. There is therefore no classical duration-of-use signal for it at all.

NO VIPAKA / GUNA / CHANNEL ENTRY / CLASSICAL INDICATIONS / PREPARATION DOCTRINE / CONTRAINDICATIONS available from any pre-1900 source. Everything the database says about maitake's traditional use is modern in origin, and the row should say so rather than back-dating it to 1596.

results.pre1900_finding: 氣味甘平無毒 — sweet, NEUTRAL (平), non-toxic. Stated in the Bencao Gangmu 1596 (attributed there to Wu Rui 吳瑞) and again, independently, by Wu Yiluo in 1757 as 甘平. Two pre-1900 witnesses, no dissent.
results.source_year: 1596 (Bencao Gangmu, Siku Quanshu recension); independently corroborated by Ben Cao Cong Xin, 1757
results.evidence: Li Shizhen 李時珍, 本草綱目 (四庫全書本) 卷二十八, 香蕈 entry, 1596: 「{{SK anchor|香蕈}}{{SK notes|日用}} … 氣味甘平無毒主治益氣不飢治風破血{{SK notes|吳瑞}}松蕈治溲濁不禁食之有効{{SK notes|菌譜}}」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E7%B6%B1%E7%9B%AE_(%E5%9B%9B%E5%BA%AB%E5%85%A8%E6%9B%B8%E6%9C%AC)/%E5%8D%B728 . Wu Yiluo 吳儀洛, 本草從新, 卷十一菜部, 香蕈 entry, 1757: 「香蕈／破血治風。／甘平。破血治風。松蕈、治溲浊不禁。」 URL: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E5%BE%9E%E6%96%B0
additions: ATTRIBUTION CORRECTION FOR THE ROW: the 1596 text itself attributes both the qi-wei and the indications to 吳瑞 (Wu Rui, 日用本草, 14th century), and heads the entry 「香蕈{{SK notes|日用}}」. So the true pre-1900 origin of the shiitake temperature is the Rihong Bencao, transmitted by Li Shizhen — not Li Shizhen's own determination and certainly not the Shennong Bencao Jing, which the stored row names as author. NO SHENNONG GRADE EXISTS: shiitake is absent from the Shennong Bencao Jing, so there is no 上品/中品/下品 signal for it, and no classical warrant for or against daily use.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS, and they are NARROW — this is the sharpest finding here. The entire pre-1900 indication list is four characters plus four: 「益氣不飢」 (augments qi, staves off hunger) and 「治風破血」 (treats wind, BREAKS BLOOD). Wu Yiluo 1757 leads with 破血治風 as the entry's one-line function summary. 破血 (breaking blood / moving blood stasis) is a MOVING, dispersing action — it is not a tonic action, and it is the opposite pole from the stored row's 'deep food-tonic that rebuilds depleted defensive Qi', 'nourishes', 'feeds the convalescent'. Nothing in either pre-1900 source says shiitake tonifies spleen qi, builds wei qi, resolves phlegm, removes toxicity, or promotes the eruption of measles. Those claims are modern and the row back-dates them to 1596.

CONTRAINDICATION IMPLIED BY 破血: a blood-breaking agent is classically withheld in pregnancy and in bleeding. The 1596 and 1757 entries do not state this for 香蕈 specifically, so I am flagging the inference, not asserting a source. What the 1596 集解 DOES warn is a collection hazard: 「生山僻處者有毒殺人」 — those growing in remote mountain places are poisonous and kill people, and Li Shizhen adds of the lookalike 鵝膏蕈 that it is easily confused with 杜蕈 (a ground fungus) and 「不可不慎」, one must not fail to be careful.
CHANNEL ENTRY (归经): NONE stated in either source. The row's assignment to Spleen, Stomach and Lung has no pre-1900 warrant.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE: the 1596 集解, quoting Chen Renyu's 菌譜, records that mountain people 「曝乾以售香味减於生者」 — sun-dried for sale, the aroma is LESS than the fresh; and for the related 稠膏蕈 gives an explicit cooking rule, 「下鼎似沸漉起…切勿攪動則涎腥不可食矣」 (drop into the pot as it comes to the boil and lift out; on no account stir, or it turns slimy-fishy and inedible). So the classical record treats fungus preparation as method-sensitive.

SPECIES: secure. The 1596 集解 描述 「蕈生桐栁枳椇木上紫色者名香蕈…香蕈生深山爛楓木上小於菌而薄黃黒色味甚香美最為佳品」 — grown on tong, willow, zhiju and rotten maple wood, thin, yellow-black, highly fragrant. That is shiitake, and the entry is distinct from 蘑菰蕈 (甘寒), 天花蕈 (甘平), 雞㙡 (甘平) and 松蕈, all of which sit in the same section and are easy to conflate.

The stored 'Warm' is right in direction but understates the classical grade, which is 大溫 not 溫. The Sanskrit stream, however, is genuinely split and cannot be collapsed: Raja Nighantu 5.65 gives वाकुची कटुतिक्तोष्णा (HOT) while Bhavaprakasha 2.207-208 gives बाकुची… हिमा (COLD).

Narahari नरहरि, राजनिघण्टुः, शताह्वादिवर्गः 6.65 (c. 13th century, Devanagari original): 「वाकुची कटुतिक्तोष्णा क्रिमिकुष्ठकफापहा । त्वग्दोषविषकण्डूतिखर्जुप्रशमनी च सा ॥ ६.६५」 URL: https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%9C%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%98%E0%A4%A3%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9F%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%83/%E0%A4%B6%E0%A4%A4%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B9%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A6%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83 . THE OPPOSING SANSKRIT READING, quoted in full so it is not buried — Bhavamishra भावमिश्र, भावप्रकाशनिघण्टुः 2.207-208 (16th century): 「बाकुची मधुरा तिक्ता कटुपाका रसायनी ॥२०७ विष्टम्भहृद्धिमा रुच्या सरा श्लेष्मास्रपित्तनुत् । रूक्षा हृद्या श्वासकुष्ठमेहज्वरकृमिप्रणुत् ॥२०८ तत्फलं पित्तलं कुष्ठकफानिलहरं कटु」 — sweet and bitter in rasa, PUNGENT IN VIPAKA, rasayana, viṣṭambha-relieving, HIMA (cold), appetising, mobile, dry; while THE FRUIT (tat-phalam) is pitta-increasing and pungent. AND THE PRE-1900 ENGLISH RECORD OF THE SAME SPLIT: William Dymock, C. J. H. Warden and David Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. I, entry PSORALIA CORYLIFOLIA, Linn., 1890, p. 412: "Native works on Materia Medica describe the seeds as hot and dry, or according to some, cold and dry, lenitive, fragrant, stimulant and aphrodisiac." URL: https://archive.org/download/b21960343_0001/b21960343_0001_djvu.txt . English glosses of the Sanskrit are my own working renderings.
additions: SPECIES TRAP, AND IT IS LOAD-BEARING FOR THE SANSKRIT EVIDENCE. Both pre-1900 Indian authorities identify the Sanskrit names Vakuchi / Somaraji / Avalguja as VERNONIA ANTHELMINTICA, not Psoralea. U. C. Dutt, The Materia Medica of the Hindus, 1877, glossary p. 318, s.v. Somaraji: "Vernonia anthelmintica Willd.", with Vakuchi cross-referenced to it; and his entry is headed "VERNONIA ANTHELMINTICA, Willd. … Sans. Somaraji, Avalguja, Vakuchi." Dymock 1891, Vol. II, likewise heads VERNONIA ANTHELMINTICA and states "Vakuchi is described in the Nighantas as sweet, pungent, digestive, bitter, alterative, astringent, COLD, cardiacal, dry, antiphlegmatic" — which is the Bhavaprakasha verse above, applied by him to Vernonia. So the 'cold' Sanskrit reading may belong to a different plant entirely. Dymock's separate Psoralea corylifolia entry, which is the one that actually matches this row's Latin binomial, calls it Lata-kasturika/Bavachi and gives "hot and dry". The database's assertion that the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas prescribe Bakuchi = Psoralea for shvitra cannot be verified from any pre-1900 source I reached, and the identification was already unsettled in 1877.

THE CHINESE STREAM IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND SPECIES-SECURE, so lean on it: BCGM 1596 集解 says 「補骨脂生嶺南諸州及波斯國」 and the 釋名 gives 「胡人呼為婆固脂而俗訛為破故紙也」 — a named foreign import with a transliterated Persian/Sanskrit name, matching Psoralea. It is 辛大温 there and 辛苦大溫 in Wu Yiluo 1757.

CHANNEL ENTRY (归经): Wu Yiluo, 本草從新, 1757: 「破故紙 一名補骨脂。燥補命火。辛苦大溫。入心包命門。補相火以通君火。」 — enters the PERICARDIUM and the MINGMEN (life gate); supplements the ministerial fire so as to communicate with the sovereign fire. Li Shizhen 1596 gives the same mechanism in the 發明: 「破故紙屬火收歛神明能使心包之火與命門之火相通故元陽堅固骨髓充實」. This channel pair is absent from the database. (BCCX URL https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E5%BE%9E%E6%96%B0 ; its transcription is mixed simplified, so locate-only.)

NO SHENNONG GRADE: 補骨脂 is not in the Shennong Bencao Jing. BCGM heads it 「宋開寳」 — it first enters the Chinese record in the Kaibao Bencao (973 CE), as an import. No 上品/中品/下品 duration signal exists. On the Indian side, Bhavaprakasha 2.207 does class it रसायनी (rasayana) and Dymock 1890 confirms "The Hindus class them with the rasāyāna or alchemic drugs."

CONTRAINDICATIONS, and they are serious — the database's own energetics_summary calls this a 'liver-taxing seed of narrow margin', and the classical record independently agrees: (1) 「墮胎」 — CAUSES MISCARRIAGE, stated in the 開寳 indication line quoted inside BCGM 1596 (「及婦人血氣墮胎」) and repeated by Wu Yiluo 1757. (2) Wu Yiluo 1757: 「陰虛有熱。大便闭结者戒之。」 — forbidden in yin deficiency with heat, and in constipation. (3) BCGM 1596: 「珣曰惡甘草」 (Li Xun: it hates liquorice) and 「時珍曰忌芸薹及諸血得胡桃胡麻良」 (Li Shizhen: AVOID rape/brassica greens and all blood [as food]; it goes well with walnut and sesame). The rape-greens and blood prohibition is a dietary contraindication with no equivalent anywhere in the modern literature, and it is repeated in the Zheng Xiangguo case history the BCGM reproduces: 「忌羊血芸苔」.

PREPARATION DOCTRINE, mandatory not optional (BCGM 1596, 子修治): 「斆曰此性燥毒須用酒浸一宿漉出以東流水浸三日夜蒸之從已至申日乾用一法以鹽同炒過曝乾用」 — Lei Xiao: THIS DRUG'S NATURE IS DRYING AND TOXIC, so it MUST be steeped in wine one night, drained, then soaked three days and nights in east-flowing water, then steamed from si to shen hour and sun-dried; alternatively fried with salt and sun-dried. Wu Yiluo 1757 gives the same set plus child's-urine and milk soaking. A raw, unprocessed seed is explicitly outside the classical doctrine — directly relevant given the modern hepatotoxicity signal.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the source's own idiom (BCGM 1596): 五勞七傷, 風虚冷, 骨髓傷敗, 腎冷精流 (開寳); 男子腰疼膝冷, 囊濕, 逐諸冷痺頑, 止小便, 腹中冷 (甄權); 興陽事, 明耳目 (大明); 治腎泄, 通命門, 煖丹田, 歛精神 (時珍). Note the classical Chinese record contains NO use for vitiligo/leukoderma — that indication comes entirely from the Indian stream (Dutt 1877 and Dymock 1890 both give it at length, Dymock quoting Kanny Loll Dey's 1881 account of repigmentation from the oleo-resinous extract).

VEHICLE DOCTRINE: the BCGM 1596 records the famous Zheng Xiangguo formula verbatim — 破故紙十兩 with 胡桃瓤二十兩 and honey, 「旦日以煖酒二合調藥一匙服of…如不飲酒人以暖熱水調之」 — taken in warm WINE at dawn, or warm water for non-drinkers. Han Feixia's rationale is given: 「故紙屬火…胡桃屬木潤燥養血…有木火相生之妙」, and the aphorism 「破故紙無胡桃猶水母之無鰕也」 — bugu zhi without walnut is like a jellyfish without its shrimp. The walnut pairing is doctrine specifically to offset the drug's dryness.

results.pre1900_finding: रूक्षोष्ण — DRY AND HOT, stated in exactly those terms. Bhavaprakasha Nighantu 2.70-71: 「चित्रकः कटुकः पाके वह्निकृत्पाचनो लघुः । रूक्षोष्णो ग्रहणीकुष्ठशोथार्शःकृमिकासनुत्」 — pungent in vipaka, fire-kindling, digestive, light, DRY-AND-HOT. Raja Nighantu 5.45 states it in the strongest classical idiom available: 「चित्रकोऽग्निसमः पाके कटुः」 — Chitraka is EQUAL TO FIRE. Both the stored temperature (Hot) and the stored moisture (Dry) are confirmed verbatim, which is unusual in this batch.
results.source_year: c. 1300 (Raja Nighantu) and 16th century (Bhavaprakasha Nighantu), Devanagari originals; corroborated by Dymock, Pharmacographia Indica Vol. II, 1891
results.evidence: Bhavamishra भावमिश्र, भावप्रकाशनिघण्टुः, हरीतक्यादिवर्ग 2.70-71 (16th century; Devanagari original, sa.wikisource): 「चित्रकोऽनलनामाच पाठी व्यालस्तथोषणः । चित्रकः कटुकः पाके वह्निकृत्पाचनो लघुः ॥२.७० रूक्षोष्णो ग्रहणीकुष्ठशोथार्शःकृमिकासनुत् । वातश्लेष्महरो ग्राही वातघ्नः श्लेष्मपित्तहृत् ॥७१」 URL: https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B6%E0%A4%83/%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%82%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%96%E0%A4%A3%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A1%E0%A5%87_%E0%A4%AD%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B6%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%98%E0%A4%A3%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9F%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%83 . Narahari नरहरि, राजनिघण्टुः, पिप्पल्यादिवर्गः 5.43-45 (c. 13th century): 「चित्रकोऽग्निश्च शार्दूलश्चित्रपाली कटुः शिखी । कृशानुर्दहनो व्यालो ज्योतिष्कः पालकस्तथा ॥५.४३ अनलो दारुणो वह्निः पावकः शबलस्तथा ॥५.४४ चित्रकोऽग्निसमः पाके कटुः शोफकफापहः । वातोदरार्शोग्रहणीक्रिमिकण्डूतिनाशनः ॥५.४५」 URL: https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%9C%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%98%E0%A4%A3%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9F%E0%A5%81%E0%A4%83/%E0%A4%AA%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AA%E0%A4%B2%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%A6%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%97%E0%A4%83 . CORROBORATION IN A PRE-1900 ENGLISH SOURCE: William Dymock, C. J. H. Warden and David Hooper, Pharmacographia Indica, Vol. II, entry PLUMBAGO ZEYLANICA, Linn., 1891, p. 329: "These plants, in Sanskrit Chitraka, are described as digestive, light, astringent, hot and appetizing; a remedy for dyspepsia, piles, leprosy, anasarca, worms, cough, phlegm, wind and biliousness. In the Nighantas, among other synonyms, they bear the names Daruna, Dahana, and Agni, in allusion to their burning and acrid properties." URL: https://archive.org/download/b21960343_0002/b21960343_0002_djvu.txt . English glosses of the Sanskrit are my own working renderings.
additions: VIPAKA, stated explicitly: कटुकः पाके / पाके कटुः — PUNGENT (katu) in vipaka, in both nighantus. The database has no vipaka column and this is a clean, unambiguous value.

GUNA: लघुः (laghu, LIGHT) and रूक्ष (ruksha, DRY) — BPN 2.70-71; Dymock 1891 renders the same pair as "light". Also ग्राही (grahi, absorbent/constipating) at BPN 2.71, which Dymock renders "astringent". Grahi is an important qualifier the row lacks: this is a hot dry stimulant that BINDS, not one that purges.

THE NAME IS ITSELF THE TEMPERATURE CLAIM. Raja Nighantu 5.43-44 lists the synonyms अग्नि (fire), शिखी (flame-crested), कृशानु (fire), दहन (burning), अनल (fire), दारुण (fearsome), वह्नि (fire-bearer), पावक (purifying fire), ज्योतिष्क (luminous), दाहक (burner). Ten of its classical names are words for fire. Dymock 1891 notices the same and glosses it "in allusion to their burning and acrid properties." No pre-1900 source dissents from hot for this plant.

CONTRAINDICATIONS, classical and grave — this fully vindicates the row's 'best kept in a practitioner's hand': (1) ABORTIFACIENT. Dymock 1891 on the Muslim (Unani) treatment of the drug as Shitaraj: "they describe it as caustic and vesicant, an expellant of phlegmatic humors; useful in rheumatism and spleen, digestive; IT ALSO CAUSES ABORTION." U. C. Dutt, 1877, p. 187, on the closely-used P. rosea: "The root of Plumbago rosea taken internally will expel the foetus from the womb, whether dead or alive." (2) CAUSTIC/VESICANT ON THE SKIN — Dymock 1891 gives the timing rule verbatim: "Such a paste may be applied externally in leprosy and other skin diseases of an obstinate character, and be allowed to remain UNTIL A BLISTER HAS FORMED. In rheumatism it should be removed after 15 to 20 minutes." A 15-to-20-minute maximum contact time is a hard classical safety limit and belongs in the row. (3) DELIBERATE ABUSE AS A CAUSTIC IS DOCUMENTED: "Religious mendicants attending fairs use the root for the purpose of raising sores upon their bodies, in order to obtain pity and alms" (Dymock 1891).

PREPARATION DOCTRINE: (a) internal dose is stated — "When administered internally the dose is one dirhem" (Dymock 1891). (b) VEHICLE MATTERS: "For external administration it is made into a paste with milk, vinegar or salt and water" (Dymock 1891). (c) THE JAR METHOD, which is a genuine dose-limiting technique and is recorded identically in both 1877 and 1891 — Dutt 1877, p. 186: "An earthen jar or pot is lined in its interior with a paste of the root, and curdled milk (dadhi) or kanjika is prepared in this pot, and taken by persons affected with haemorrhoids, and prurigo." The patient never swallows the root; only what leaches into the curd. That is classical harm-reduction and the database has no field for it. NOTE: the row's part_used says the root is 'purified (shodhita) before internal use' — I could NOT verify a shodhana procedure for Chitraka in any pre-1900 source I reached. The jar method and the milk/vinegar paste are what the pre-1900 record actually specifies. Treat 'shodhita' as unverified.

CLASSICAL COMPOUND FORMULAS, named in the pre-1900 record: TRIMADA — plumbago root, Embelia ribes fruit and Cyperus tubers (Dutt 1877 p. 186; Dymock 1891 p. 329). SHADDHARANA YOGA, "an old prescription of Susruta's" — equal parts plumbago root, indrayava (Holarrhena), patha (Cissampelos/Stephania), Picrorhiza kurroa, atis (Aconitum heterophyllum) and chebulic myrobalan, dose about one drachm (both sources). PANCHAKOLA — BPN 2.72: 「पिप्पली पिप्पलीमूलं चव्यचित्रकनागरैः पञ्चभिः कोलमात्रं यत्पञ्चकोलं तदुच्यते」, i.e. Chitraka is one of the five pungents, and 2.73 calls the group तीक्ष्णोष्णं (sharp and hot). Chitraka is almost never a solo herb in the classical record.

CLASSICAL INDICATIONS in the sources' own idiom: BPN 2.70-71 — वह्निकृत् (kindles the digestive fire), पाचन (digestive); destroys ग्रहणी (sprue/malabsorption), कुष्ठ, शोथ (oedema), अर्शः (piles), कृमि (worms), कास (cough); removes vata and kapha, and is ग्राही. RN 5.45 — removes शोफ and कफ; destroys वातोदर (flatulent abdomen), अर्शः, ग्रहणी, क्रिमि, कण्डूति (itching). RN 5.47 on the red variety रक्तचित्रक adds स्थूलकायकरः (body-building), रुच्यः, कुष्ठघ्नः, रसायनः.

SPECIES NOTE: the pre-1900 record does not cleanly separate P. zeylanica from P. rosea. Dymock 1891 heads the article PLUMBAGO ZEYLANICA, Linn. but treats P. rosea in the same entry and warns "The Shitaraj of Mahometan writers must, therefore, be considered to refer to the GENUS Plumbago, and not to any particular species", adding that P. rosea "is said to be more active" and that P. zeylanica "very possibly may have been used by some under the supposition that it was the root of P. rosea." Dutt 1877 keeps them as separate entries (Chitraka vs Raktachitraka) and assigns P. rosea a specific uterine action absent from P. zeylanica. Any potency or abortifacient claim carried across from rosea to zeylanica is an over-read.
